Furthermore, what the Government has been saying over the last couple of weeks and what the Prime Minister has been saying over the last couple of days is also unacceptable. Mr. Chairman, 1 rise to respond very briefly to this amendment and to indicate, unfortunately, what has happened with respect to it. When we look through all the political rhetoric which has gone into the presentation of this
particular amendment, we discover that the Opposition is now suggesting that there be a limit with respect to very clearly laid down, unprecedented borrowing authority legislation which has come before the House in an appropriate manner, as we brought down the Estimates with respect to the spending requirements of the Government of Canada. A proposition with respect to the borrowing requirements of the country was brought in within two days of the Budget in order to ensure that essential services can be provided by the Government of Canada through a borrowing authority. This particular borrowing authority is justified on the basis of the statistics provided within the Budget and the Estimates which have been laid before the House.
On occasion, the Opposition attempts to make political points. As we in the House of Commons say, this is a political forum, but let us consider the effect of this particular amendment. By virtue of this particular amendment, the Official Opposition is saying that every person who relies on expenditures through the federal Government will be cut by 3 per cent more than is now required by the Government of Canada to carry on under the terms of its Budget. It is saying to the people of Canada that they will be cut more. It is saying to Canadians who rely on payments, subsidies, grants and a variety of things, that they now have to take a reduction. These are the same Members who are complaining about a process under which the Government will modify indexing in the future and which, we say to the people of Canada, we are monitoring on an ongoing basis. The Opposition says: "No, cut the poor right now". This goes right to the people in society least able to defend themselves. The Opposition is now saying: "Cut the amount of money you are now spending on the poor of the country". This is the effect of its amendment.

Mr. Chairman, I have listened very carefully to the intervention of the Hon. Government House Leader. In his attempt to lecture us he has overlooked a very important point, which is not unusual in his myopic approach to politics. He has inadvertently, or perhaps inaccurately, accused us of slashing borrowing authority. He does not seem to realize that the Liberal Opposition is putting pressure on the Government at the first opportunity available for us to do our job and to speak up. Contrary to what the Government House Leader said, we have listened to the signals that we have received from pensioners across the nation.
As the weeks pass, it becomes quite clear that this is an important issue of national dimension. On May 23, the Minister of Finance said that there would be deindexation. He did not say that there may be deindexation; he said that there
Borrowing Authority Act
would be deindexation. He also said that there would be deindexation of family allowances. He did not say that there may be deindexation of family allowances; he said that there would be such deindexation. Now all of a sudden, the Prime Minister is saying that that was just a proposal and that we should not be upset. He says we should not interpret "will" as meaning "will", that it may mean "may". For the first time in recent history the Budget is no longer a Budget. It is something which ressembles a White Paper. The pensioners of Canada and those who are approaching that time of life are thinking that perhaps they should not take seriously what the Minister of Finance is saying. Perhaps they should wait for potential statements from the Prime Minister. As every day goes by, the distance between those two gentlemen is growing.
If I were a Tory back-bencher, God forbid, I would have to ask myself what I would say to my constituents during July and August. Are they going to tell their constituents what the Minister of Finance said on May 23, or what the Prime Minister has been saying in the last few weeks? What is the true theology? That is the question facing 180 inexperienced back-benchers who will face the music when they go home. I feel sympathy for them because it is the first time in a long time that they will have to defend government policies. The people of their constituencies are wondering what on earth is going on.
An issue of national importance has emerged. The Official Opposition has seized the issue because it is its duty. If Conservative Members were in opposition they would be doing the same thing. We are asking the Government to diminish the amount of money which is requested in the borrowing authority Bill by the amount of the proposed deindexing. We are on our toes in the Official Opposition and we are putting pressure on the Government, at the first opportunity, with this amendment. That is what we are doing.

I feel obliged to point out the logic. Borrowing authority provides the Government with the opportunity to meet its obligations. These obligations are not just to senior citizens, they are, in the main, to bankers because of the spendthrift activities of the previous Government during the last 20 years. What those Hon. Members opposite are doing by asking us to decrease the borrowing authority of the Government-and the bankers, of course, will want their pound of flesh-is to decrease the Government's ability to meet its obligation to the poor, because we will be paying the bankers and our other statutory obligations to the provinces.
What those Hon. Members should have done, if they had wanted to be responsible and if anything else but their selfish political motives had motivated them, would have been to increase the borrowing authority with the view to the Government's proceeding with the reindexation of pensions. We could have debated that logically. But what they have done now, if in fact their motion carries, is to make it necesssary to renege on other social programs, because that is the only thing we can renege on. We cannot renege on our obligations to the foreign bankers. There is no money tree out in the backyard. These thousands of people who come from all across Canada and the United States are walking around these buildings thinking there are money trees out in the back. There are no money trees. The Government cannot give anything away that it has not first taken from somewhere else. Had it not been for the strange and irresponsible policies of the Liberal Government over the last 20 years, we would not be in this fix.
So I appeal to the Opposition's sense of fairness and logic. What it is doing makes absolutely no sense at all. What it should be doing is to increase the spending authority. Mind you, we would fight this. I speak to senior citizens as well. They built this country. They put us where we are. And something else they did throughout their lives is to have paid their bills, something which the Liberal Government did not do. Had it done that, we would not be in the fix we are in. The senior citizens who write to me say, "For God's sake, pay your bills because we don't want to pass our debts on to our grandchildren".
I appeal to the Opposition's sense of logic and fairness, Mr. Speaker, and I would like to think that it would withdraw this motion.

Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of the debate on this amendment, I think it would be a good thing to explain clearly what the intentions are of the
Opposition and our reason for moving an amendment that seems to have taken our friends opposite by surprise.
Mr. Chairman, the reason is quite simple. Ever since a Budget we consider unfair and inequitable was brought down, we have tried in every possible way to make Government Members understand that in an enlightened society like ours, we cannot tolerate any attempt to reduce the deficit by making the rich richer and putting a greater burden on the neediest in our society, and I am referring to those people who only have their Old Age Security pension and especially those who have to live on that pension plus the Guaranteed Income Supplement.
We know that Canadians who are receiving the Old Age Security pension and the Guaranteed Income Supplement are those who are living below the poverty line across this country. We cannot accept this, and we have said it a hundred times over. However, our efforts together with those of thousands of Canadians across the country do not seem to have moved the Government away from its determination to make people pay who cannot afford to pay.
That is why we are moving this motion this morning, in an attempt to make the Government take its own medicine so it will understand that a 3 per cent cut in income is not something to be taken lightly.
We realize the Government must meet its commitments. That is why it has tabled a Bill to seek borrowing authority, which means that the Government can then go to the financial markets and borrow the funds it needs for its operations. We think that if the Government does not realize what a three per cent cut in income means to the neediest in Canada, perhaps it will understand-although I am not so sure-when it has to take a 3 per cent cut in its borrowing authority, that a three per cent cut can hurt. And that is why we are taking this action.

We are just trying to impress on this Government that a 3 per cent cut when one is below the poverty line is unacceptable. And after repeating this hundreds of times it is obvious that we have not so far been able to push our message across. So we are trying, by a practical amendment, to let the Government feel the pinch of a 3 per cent cut, and that is the reason we are doing it.
When the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River, who is hurling invective at me, said earlier that there was no logic in what we are doing because if we had wanted to reindex pensions we should have moved an increase in the borrowing authority not a decrease, he proved that he does not understand the way this Budget and the borrowing authority work.

What you are doing is taking more from those who need it most. It has been

termed a proposal, not a measure anymore. Why write it in the budget documents in the first place? It could have monitored the economic situation, and if it thought at the end of the year there was reason to cut the pension indexation, it could have done so without having the seniors worry for months over what it was going to do.
What the people are asking themselves at this time is whether they are going to be cut or not. So why do it? 1 am going to tell Members opposite why it was done. I know why. Maybe that will bring it back to its senses and make it do something sensible for the people who need it most.

Mr. Chairman, that is what we are trying to do by presenting this amendment. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to have an opportunity to make a few comments as a result of the unexpected turn of events here today. Yesterday, in one of the comments that I was making about Clause 2 of this borrowing Bill, 1 suggested to the Minister of State for Finance that obviously the Government had come to the conclusion that it could live with reducing the purchasing power of senior citizens by 3 per cent. A number of Conservative spokesmen have said that they are concerned and did not like to do this but it is something that had to be done. They were confident that senior citizens would support this act of cutting 3 per cent from their disposable income in the years ahead.
When we put this into dollar and cent terms, assuming that inflation remains at the stable level at which it has been for the last number of years, which all projections indicate, a typical senior citizen in our country would lose approximately $ 1,500 of purchasing power over the next five years. It also means, as the finance officials have indicated, that 220,000 senior citizens will drop below the poverty line, as defined by the Government, in the years ahead.
The Government is saying that it supports the decision to reduce senior citizens' purchasing power by 3 per cent. It believes that seniors could live with this reduction, and it is prepared to impose that upon the people who built this country.
I appreciate the symbolism of the motion put forward by the Hon. Member for Newfoundland in which he suggests that if the Government is going to ask senior citizens, as a special group, to take a 3 per cent cut, then it is not unreasonable to expect the Government itself to take a 3 per cent cut in this particular borrowing authority, which amounts to a little over half a billion dollars. Perhaps the Government itself should adjust its priorities as it has asked seniors to adjust their eating, travelling and day-to-day priorities. This motion asks the Government to adjust its expectations downward, just as it is asking senior citizens to do. I do not believe that this is an unreasonable expectation when one uses the same logic that is used by Members opposite.
Quite frankly, I have not been able to understand why there has not been outrage from Members opposite, particularly from the Hon. Member for Mississauga South who used to sit on this side of the House beside the NDP. I recall the time when he would become extremely animated in his outrage because of the discriminatory activities of the Government of the day against the oil companies. I admire the colour the Hon. Member brings to his speeches, as only he can. He went on for days and days during Question Period and in debates fighting for the oil companies because the Government, through Petro-Canada, was acting unfairly. The Hon. Member, along with some of his colleagues, convinced the Official Opposition at that time to shut down the House of Commons during the infamous bell ringing period incident because the oil companies were being punished. The Opposition at that time stayed out in the lounge and drank coffee,
June 18, 1985

talking about the importance of that act of symbolism. They believed it was important to close down Canada's Parliament in the best interest of the multinational oil companies.
While I understood their action at that time, for many reasons I did not believe it was appropriate. I did not think the priority of closing down the House of Commons to prevent free debate from taking place was appropriate. I did not appreciate the tactics because I thought they were rather dictatorial.
However, the Opposition at that time felt strongly about that issue. I cannot believe that Hon. Members opposite do not feel as strongly now about what the Government is doing to senior citizens in this Country. They are not like oil companies with headquarters in Houston and Dallas, Texas. These are hundreds of thousands of grandparents, mothers and fathers and relatives and friends who will have their disposable incomes cut.
The Minister of Finance termed these cuts within his Budget fair. However, it has been demonstrated time and again that this Budget is not fair. The Budget is punitive toward the poor of Canada because it raises taxes to the poor and middle-income Canadians while being a bonanza for the wealthy. I realize that some Members opposite smile at that remark, implying that I am wrong in that analysis. However, it is not my analysis but that of every financial analyst, business and academic economist in the country. The simple fact is that the wealthy benefit while the low and middle-income earners pay.
This country is in desperate need of leadership, as was shown when the people of Canada cried out for strong, decisive leadership in the last election.

Even if one makes a bad decision, I suppose people appreciate the fact that one believes it is correct. We have
Borrowing Authority Act
hung the poor Minister of Finance so far out on the limb that it does not matter what he does, he will fall off. If he does not, he surely should. Obviously the Prime Minister has no confidence in him. Obviously the Government of Canada has no confidence in him. I have not heard Hon. Members opposite leaping up in their places and saying: "Listen, if he does not fight for senior citizens, I am prepared to". They have been mute over there. When a Budget is brought in which cuts the expected increases to the OAS so that the purchasing power of senior citizens will be reduced next year, the year after and the year after, that, what happens to all those folk who are not senior citizens today? Before resuming my seat, I want to make one suggestion. If this particular amendment passes, it will cut a number of dollars from the borrowing authority. Yesterday we asked the officials of the Minister of State for Finance what the deferred corporate taxes were for last year. The answer we received is that they were somewhere in the neighbourhood of $30 billion, just under $30 billion, back in 1982. Something to consider, in terms of deficit reduction or obtaining more funds for social programs, is that the Government could levy a 10 per cent interest rate on deferred taxes so that corporations, instead of putting off their taxes year after year, pay just 10 per cent for that privilege. This would net us $3 billion this year. Then we would not have to worry about the 3 per cent cut to the increases in the OAS. It would even allow the Government to decrease the deficit somewhat. It would allow the Government other money, so that it would not have to impose user-fees in a number of federal areas. I step down, having made that modest proposal-impose a 10 per cent levy on deferred corporate taxes, which would result in a flow into the national Treasury of about $3 billion.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, at the beginning of this day an amendment was presented to reduce the borrowing authority by 3 per cent as a symbol to remind the Government of the onerous punishment which it has put upon the backs of senior citizens by cutting at a rate of 3 per cent of the increase in their inflation protection. This Party was trying to make one point. If the Government wants to talk about reducing deficits, then perhaps, through the symbol of cutting its spending, it would be induced, if it had 3 per cent less, to cut out some of the fat with which it has started to bloat since it became the Government in terms of patronage and of the salaries to people who were its back-bench supporters in the past. Perhaps it could cut away some of the people in the PMO which were added on, this huge number of extra employees. Perhaps it could cut back on some of the political commissars which have been placed in the offices of every Minister of the Crown in order to ensure that its particular interests are carried out for political purposes rather than in the interests of the Public Service, that is, to serve the people. It could cut in many places and be cut back to some kind of integrity. That 3 per cent might make government Members more honest.
When the Hon. House Leader rose to reply to the proposal to cut back government borrowing by 3 per cent, it was amazing that the first thing he said to the Liberal side of the House was: "You want to do this to the poor". Honni soit qui mal y pensel It is interesting that the Hon. Government House Leader did not think, when 3 per cent was to come off the Government's budget, of cutting the extra people in the PMO or of cutting patronage. The first thing which crossed his mind was obviously that if there was to be a 3 per cent cut, it would be on the backs of the poor. They would first select the poor as the targets, not the rich. It is interesting, is it not? Honni soit qui mal y pense\ In pointing the finger at us, the first thing he
thought he would have to cut as a result of a 3 per cent cut in borrowing would be the poor. That is all the Tories can think of-to cut the poor. They are their first targets.
Also it was interesting that the Hon. Member for Prince George-Peace River suggested that we should have proposed an increase in the borrowing rather than a decrease. First, the rules do not allow it. Obviously this veteran Member of the House does not understand its rules. The borrowing authority could not be increased by a proposal or motion from this side because it is not permitted. He was not interested in why we were introducing this proposal. He was trying to say that we were being hypocrites, when in reality the opposite was the case.
Also it is interesting that the Budget hits the poor and protects, and in fact gives a windfall, to the rich. The Budget offers a $500,000 lifetime opportunity in respect of capital gains. In effect, it is a gift of $125,000 in due course to everyone in the top 4 per cent of the population who invests in stock and makes other kinds of investments about which the remaining 96 per cent or 97 per cent of the Canadian population knows nothing. Instead of thinking about how they might fulfil their election promise that the rich who are paying no taxes would start to pay, they broke that promise.
We waited for nine months for this Budget to be tabled, but there was still nothing in it to ensure that the rich who had not been paying any taxes would now pay them. This borrowing authority Bill does not indicate the amount to be used for expenditures. It simply indicates the amount of money the Government will get. The Government could cut down its expenditures or increase income revenues by adjusting the Budget. The Government could introduce a Bill which would ensure that those who are paying no taxes would have to pay them from now on.
There is reason for us to be bemused and annoyed with the righteous indignation of the Hon. House Leader, who stands up in pious and pretended self-righteous indignation saying that we should stop trying to take 3 per cent away from the poor, when it is the Government that first wanted to take it from the poor. The seniors are asked to take a 3 per cent cut in the inflation protection which was introduced by the Liberal Government. The Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition introduced this measure to ensure that seniors would be protected. In the Budget, the Tory Government guarantees that the first 3 per cent of inflation will come off the backs of senior citizens. If inflation continues through the decades, as the Minister of Finance predicts it will, the first 3 per cent of inflation will be taken off the backs of senior citizens, and that rate will be compounded. It is tragic that the purchasing power of senior citizens will be threatened.
The Prime Minister said that nothing has yet happened to the senior citizens. That is a tragic way to speak to senior citizens. Something has happened to them, they are scared. Those who are too proud to ask for welfare or the GIS will fall deeper and deeper into poverty. Even with the GIS, they are
June 18, 1985

only receiving $7,000. In communities with a population of over 500,000, the poverty line is around $10,000. These people are already living $3,000 below the poverty line. Imagine what it means to senior citizens to be told that they will lose 3 per cent a year. The Prime Minister can say that nothing has happened to them yet and that perhaps the Government will change its mind, but the cuts are in the Budget and in its thoughts. The first thought of the Tories is to take away from the weak and give to the rich, the corporations, and the oil companies.
There was money in the Budget for the rich, but it was taken away from the seniors. The Government is also planning to take away from mothers. Think especially of what 3 per cent per year means to a single mother. The Government wants to take from those who cannot fight back, from the unorganized. The business lobbies are well organized, well-heeled, and have good lines of communication. The Government thought the seniors would lie down and take it.
Even those who have hesitated to become politically active realize that there must be some kind of morality in Government. During the election campaign, the Prime Minister promised the seniors that he would not take anything away from them. Now, in the first Budget, they have been betrayed. They feel this is too much. I challenge the Tory back-benchers to demand that these people be relieved of their anxiety now rather than during the summer when it would be easy for the Government to give some small token to the seniors to make them feel a little better. They are feeling bad and are worrying now. They want to be relieved of their anxiety and terror now.
Every Member of the House has received phone calls and letters from senior citizens. They know that what I am saying is true. They know of the anguish of the seniors and of the children who are worried about their parents. This is a matter of national concern. For the Prime Minister to say that nothing has happened to them is wrong. A lot has happened to them. They have been shaken up and threatened. Their futures have been put in jeopardy. To suggest another 3 per cent cut to those who are already living in poverty is drastic, tragic, and cruel.
The Government has also made promises with regard to the give and take proposal. Before and during the election campaign the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State promised that the Government would bring forward the give and take program to give charities a 50 per cent tax credit. That promise was broken. The Government broke its promise to charities, but kept its promise to oil companies. The promise to the oil companies was a sacred trust because the first priority of the Tories is to look after the rich. However, the charity organizations which serve the churches and poor people were fobbed off without any reference in the Budget. The former Tory Budget of the present Secretary of State for External Affairs at least contained a footnote indicating that the give and take proposal would be studied. There is not even a reference to it in this Budget. The promise which the Prime Minister made to the charity organizations of the country was broken, but money was found for the oil companies. That
Borrowing Authority Act
shows the sense of values of this Government. It takes from the poor and gives to the rich. Premier Buchanan said that this was politically unsound. They were told by Premier Miller that this was politically unsound. Yet they have the amazing audacity to think that they could put this one over on the Canadian people and that the Canadian people would accept it. To think that they can give money to the oil companies and a windfall of $125,000 to 4 per cent of the population, while taking away from the poor is sheer arrogance. It is arrogant to think that the people of Canada would stand for it.
I am sorry that I have to rise to speak in this way about the Government. It sounds as though 1 were over-simplifying the matter. I thought that perhaps there might have been some amelioration in the situation. The more I study the Budget and see its repercussions, the more I am amazed at the Government for giving to the rich and taking from the poor.
The Government took away from the charities. As well, it broke promises in other areas. It broke its promises to senior citizens. The Prime Minister promised that this would never happen. It broke its promises in terms of universality. It broke its promises to the charities of the country and its promises to the disabled and women. Just today, the press is reporting on how women's organizations are protesting that they too have been betrayed.
Is there no shame on the part of the Government? Did government Members think that because the Budget would come out in the late spring, the summer would soon come and they could escape scot-free? I hope the Canadian people will keep this very much in mind all during the summer. We can guarantee to them that when the fall comes, they will still be facing the same problems.
The fundamental problem is this: the Government had better decide that it must keep its election promises. It had better decide that if it wants to survive, it should listen to the people and care as much for the poor as it does for the rich.

Are they going to recommend that the Cabinet take action by announcing to the seniors of the country that their cry has reached the Cabinet

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
and that it intends to do something about their suffering? Will they ask the Government to reinstate the 3 per cent that it has deindexed from the pensions? I hope that at the same time the Government will also reconsider its position on family allowances for those who are poor. As well, I hope the Government will listen to the voices in Atlantic Canada that have expressed their horror at what is being proposed by this Budget.
In Atlantic Canada, there are certain regional disparities and the area requires and depends upon federal transfers and grants. The people in Atlantic Canada are saying that the Budget will hurt their communities and particularly the disadvantaged ones. This is again another case of the federal Government's Budget being one that attacks those who are poor and weak who live in the disadvantaged provinces while giving to those who live in the wealthy provinces.
The Government's record is an amazing one. As the people of Canada study it, they will better understand the philosophy of the Tory Party. I understand even more clearly now after the Budget why I became a member of the Liberal Party. 1 hope that the Government will take steps that will take into account this motion to cut back government borrowing by 3 per cent and look at the way it is spending money on things that are fat and unimportant. I hope that it will give back that 3 per cent which is causing such anguish to the poor seniors.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to pay tribute to the speech that has been given by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence. He has, in a very articulate and obviously passionate way, restated the kind of appreciation that he has from a human point of view for the anxieties and worries felt by senior citizens who are struggling to meet their commitments resulting from the Government's 3 per cent reduction.
The Hon. Member for Eglinton-Lawrence has perhaps seen more clearly and understands more clearly than most the mentality of the Government. He made a very important point when he said that the Opposition has moved a 3 per cent reduction in the Government's borrowing authority as a very symbolic gesture of the kind of arbitrary manner in which the Government is treating senior citizens. Speaking on behalf of all government Members, what does the Government House Leader say to that?
This motion would reduce the Government's borrowing authority by less than $600 million. In fact, the Government could cancel or limit capital gains exemptions to save that much money. However, what does the Government House Leader say? Does he say that this motion may require the Government to reduce the capital gains give-away? Does he say that this may require the Government to reduce by one-third the amount of money it is giving back to the multinational oil companies? Does he say that this will require the Government to return to the old levels the salaries of chiefs of staffs, of commissars and of Ministers, or to reduce office furniture budgets? Does he ask Ministers not to trade in their cars every six months? No, he does not.
What does the Government House Leader say as an immediate response to the motion to reduce borrowing authority by about half a billion dollars? He says that we will have to cut back on the poor, and he is speaking on behalf of 211 Members of Parliament who wear the Conservative stripe. He says that when there is any discussion of cutting back on government expenditures, we should cut back on the poor.
This 3 per cent reduction represents about a half a billion dollars. Half a billion dollars represents about one-third of the cost of giving $125,000 in cash gifts to the rich of this country. The 3 per cent reduction could be absorbed without cutting any social programs. The 3 per cent reduction could be absorbed, the capital gains provision could be scrapped and there would be a billion dollars left over to give to senior citizens. This could be done if the minds, hearts and souls of government Members were concerned with how the poor people of this country live. This could be done if government Members had any basic respect for the people who built this country. This could be done if government Members were not beholden to the wealthy economic interests as represented by multinational oil companies and banks and the kinds of people who bankrolled their Party in the last federal election campaign.
We have proposed this kind of measures because for the last three weeks, as we debated and asked questions about the Government's deindexation plan and as we listened to senior citizens of the country speak about it, our caucus met-and I am not supposed to tell secrets out of caucus-but there we indicated that we believed that the back-benchers, the rank and file of the Conservative Party, would make their voices heard. We believed that they would make their presence felt. We believed that even if the Cabinet, in some kind of kamikaze mission, saved the so-called honour of the Minister of Finance by not backing away and even if the Cabinet insisted on committing hara-kiri on public television, those backbenchers who had gone to talk to their constituents and to their own mothers, fathers and grandparents would have made their presence felt. We believed that those back-benchers would have made their presence and influence felt. We thought that during the past weekend at the special emergency caucus meeting of the Conservative Party, which was called to keep the caucus from disintegrating over the issue, the voice of the people of Canada as represented by back-benchers would be heard, and that it would not be the voice of Cabinet as represented by the Prime Minister that would carry the day. We thought there would be an announcement on Saturday or Sunday that the Government would move away from deindexing. However, it was not the voice of the back-benchers which carried the day. It was not the voice of those who truly have the power in Parliament-the majority of Members who sit on the back-benches. They were stifled. They were beaten back by the bullies in the Cabinet. They were told, in the name of the honour and prestige of the Minister of Finance, to bite their tongues.
I know Tory back-benchers. I know they are not happy. 1 do not have to ask them if they are upset. I do not have to ask them whether they agree. I know there are a substantial
June 18, 1985

number of Tory back-benchers who do not agree with the policy. I know them well enough to know that their voices were heard lound and clear at the caucus meeting. I know them well enough to know that they rose and stated their points of view. I know that they urged the Prime Minister and the Cabinet to do the right thing. Perhaps they are as shocked as I am to realize that not only will Cabinet not listen to the Opposition, organized groups in the country, the Chamber of Commerce, business institutions, social councils, provincial Premiers and provincial Conservative Parties, but that it also will not listen to its own back-benchers.
Reform of the House cannot come quick enough. We have a Prime Minister who ignored the pleas from his back-benchers on Saturday. That is no secret. He cracks the whip and tells them to sit quietly in their seats. There is something wrong. The biggest worry which the people of Canada had on September 5 was that there was too big a majority and that too much power had been placed in the hands of one man and his Cabinet. We have an administration which is a collection of 39 men and women who will not be policed by the voice of their back-benchers. We have a Government which has assumed the arrogance of a dictatorship. We have a Government which is made up of Members who believe that it is more important that they never have to say they are sorry because they are Tories. They will not relieve the senior citizens of the country of the burden of anxiety and the weight of not knowing whether in one, two, three or five years they will have not only Old Age Security payments, but security in their old age.
I find it incredible that the Government is asking for borrowing authority in the amount of $18.2 billion. It would take 18 Canadians spending $1,000 a day for 3,000 years, to spend that amount of money. We have proposed that it should be cut by 3 per cent. The Government has told us that it cannot do that because it has commitments and bills which must be paid. The Government is saying that we cannot arbitrarily cut its spending program by 3 per cent because it has commitments. What a brilliant defence! It sounds familiar. That is what the senior citizens of the country have been saying to the Government. The Government did not consult with them nor did it assess what would be the impact. It arbitrarily cut the budgets of senior citizens by 3 per cent. The senior citizens have told the Government that it cannot do that because they have commitments to meet. The Government responded by saying no. The Government tells them that they are happy to participate. The Government tells us that it has spoken to one or two senior citizens and that they are happy to participate. If that is not hypocrisy, what is?
The Prime Minister visited his riding. His staff spent several weeks trying to orchestrate carefully a good reception. They went into a poll which he had won overwhelmingly in the last election-Le Pionnier. His staff thought that Le Pionnier would be safe turf. The overwhelming majority of people in Le Pionnier, in the Prime Minister's riding, and in senior citizens' complexes, voted for the Prime Minister. His staff thought that it would be a safe media event. They thought it was a safe place for the Prime Minister to bring his presidential podium

and his travelling troup in order to show the people of Canada, by way of a media event, that there is no problem with the deindexing measure.
This morning in The Gazette and in the French press we read that those senior citizens used very strong language to describe the Prime Minister. In fact, I am upset. I think it is terrible for senior citizens in the Prime Minister's riding to gang up on him. They used language which I would never use. They called the Prime Minister a liar. I do not accept that. Those senior citizens could have found another word to describe what the Prime Minister did to them. When they use that kind of blunt, honest and simple language, we cannot repeat it in the House. An 82-year old man, who voted for the Prime Minister, said that the Prime Minister had lied to him. Is that an indicator? Could we call that putting the finger on the pulse and discovering that people are not happy? The Prime Minister does not. He said that he was pleased with the warm reception which he received.
Tory back-benchers have a rare opportunity to show their constituents that, as well as being members of the Conservative caucus and the Prime Minister's soldiers, they have their ears tuned to what their constituents are saying. Tory backbenchers have the opportunity to show their constituents that they have their fingers on the pulse of life's blood as it beats through their constituencies. They should show their constituents that they are prepared to stand up and be the Members of Parliament for their ridings. They should be prepared once in a while to be the spokesmen to Ottawa and in Ottawa from their districts, rather than just people who spend time apologizing to their constituents on behalf of Ottawa when the Government loses touch.
The Government had better consider that it is being served notice now if its intention is to keep the Prime Minister busy and out of Ottawa, and to send the Minister of Finance on a two or three-week exotic travel excursion in Europe, and not have anyone in the House to answer questions. The Government is trying to bamboozle members of the Opposition. It is treating, with total disregard and disrespect, the senior citizens of the country who are asking for an answer. The Government had better assume that it has been served notice.
We in the Opposition have no intention of allowing this kind of charade and farce to continue. We will not allow this House, the people's House, to be turned into a charade while the Prime Minister totes around his presidential podium doing media events. There are 71 Members of the Opposition and a massive majority of 211 Members of Government. I warn those Members of the Government now that the eyes of the people of this country are upon all of us. They are weighing our actions and measuring our words. We are prepared to see that this place does not work at all before its works as a charade or merely as some kind of propaganda tool for a Government who sadly, after nine months in power, is so out of touch with the realities in this country.

June 18, 1985

While the senior citizens of this country organize, prepare their position and make their way to Ottawa to come face to face with Members of Parliament and this Government, what is the Government obsessed with? Is it obsessed with doing the right thing? Is it going to dig down deep and screw up its courage and backbone and say "We made a mistake and we'll correct it right away"? No, Mr. Chairman, it is obsessed with having the Solicitor General appoint his fine buddy in the RCMP to a patronage position. It is obsessed with having Mr. Byron, who has been apppointed to the advertising committee, name the firm of which he was vice-president until a few months ago, so it can give it four or five untendered contracts. The Government is behaving like a child too long denied access to the cookie jar and it is using the taxpayers' money in a gluttonous display of greed and petty villainy while it turns a deaf ear to the 2.5 million senior citizens of this country who are demanding not special treatment, but only that the system which gave them some measure of security in their old age be restored.
Members of the Opposition rose in their places last week and told Members of the Government that we would not demand the resignation of the Minister of Finance, that we would not ask for the head of the Prime Minister and we would go quietly into a summer recess if they would but admit what they are doing is wrong and move to immediately correct the situation. There was an unpartisan mood last week. There was a time in this House when no blood was being asked for and no one was measuring the Gallup poll. We were asking for simple justice and for a display of dignity, courage and concern for justice, but that was not forthcoming. This Government is stonewalling. It is determined to make a mockery of this institution until June 30, and then to adjourn this House. Those Members will go away for the summer, leaving seniors with the anxiety of not knowing what their fate will be.
I say through you, Mr. Chairman, to the Government House Leader, who thinks if we have to cut $500 million, we have got to cut it from the poor rather than from Tory friends who are going to benefit from no capital gains tax, that the Government can easily take a few dollars back from the multinational oil companies. The Government can easily police itself and cut its extravagant spending on Ministers' offices, chauffeur-driven cars and high salaried politically appointed staff. It can make cuts to the Government jet aircraft which trounce all across the land carrying Members of the Government who are trying to sell something which is not saleable because it is not just. I warn the Government that if it continues to perpetrate this farce upon this institution, this institution will not be party to it.
It is the first responsibility of any Opposition to be the defender and scrutineer of the public purse when the public purse is being raided to provide $1.4 billion in windfall money to multinational oil companies, and when the public purse is being raided to give $125,000 to every wealthy Canadian, which is a gift from the taxpayers of Canada to those who can afford take advantage of no capital gains tax. That program is going to cost as much as the Government is taking away from
senior citizens, and the Opposition cannot sit quietly as Government reaches out and tries to pay for that giveaway by taking it from the group which is the most defenceless and which cannot speak for themselves, the senior citizens. If the Government believes it can roll this group like a mugger in a park and there will no outcry, then the Opposition cannot be silent. This institution will not function as a farce.

Mr. Chairman, I am also pleased to rise in my place and address the motion which was tabled earlier this morning by a Member of our Opposition Party. It is again unfortunate that the Government of the day has missed the opportunity to understand and take with a certain degree of seriousness and sensitivity the message, because it is a clear message. It is a message which is not necessarily coming from this side of the House. It is a message from the millions upon millions of senior citizens across this country who have been trying to communicate by phone, petition, rally, or whatever means they can. It is a message which the senior citizens are trying to articulate with some degree of sensitivity and compassion in order to make this Government understand that what it has done through its Budget measure in taking away three percentage points from the pensions is not only wrong fiscally but wrong morally.
We in the Opposition are trying to be a vehicle for the senior citizens. We are trying to bring to this Government the understanding that its decision is absolutely dead wrong and that it has an opportunity to correct that wrong by admitting
it.
Members of this Party have been told by senior citizens, and I was told specifically at a community meeting at my constituency office last Saturday, that the senior citizens are asking "How does the Government feel when it arbitrarily and immediately cuts our pensions and how would it feel if the money which it needs to operate the business of the day was cut just as immediately and arbitrarily". The message is clear. They are saying, "Why can the Government do it so easily to senior citizens?" I suppose they were thought to be a group which was unorganized and it would be easy to make the move. It was a move which was certainly not contemplated, perhaps, against the more elitist and organized groups of this country because as soon as we touch the bankers or the corporate community, they are there the next day, organized, financed and articulate, and the Government responds.
The Government thought, perhaps, that pensions was an area in which it could afford to save some money because our senior citizens are not organized, they are not articulate, and do not have the resources nor the energy to come to Ottawa and tell this Government it is wrong. However, the senior citizens are organized, they are articulate and they do have the moral compassion to stand up and be heard. It is that Government and Party that is wrong. It is that Party that does not have the courage to stand up and say they were wrong. It is a lesson the Government ought to learn.
June 18, 1985

This motion is another way of informing the Government that it ought to rethink this proposal. Government Members say we are practising the politics of fear. We are not. That fear came from page 17 of the federal Budget which says that we are reducing the indexation of their pensions. That is where the fear started and we are trying to dispel that fear. We are trying to tell the Government to admit it is wrong, do so quickly, and remove the fear so that the senior citizens can go back to living their lives without having to worry about whether the money they rely on will remain intact.
As my colleague indicated earlier, perhaps the Prime Minister and the Government do not see the other side of the tracks. Perhaps the Prime Minister prefers to view this country as a shining city on a hill. Well, that is true; we are a privileged society. We have a good country. But there is another side of the tracks.
There is another city, and perhaps this is A Tale of Two Cities which the Prime Minister cannot understand. From where he is standing perhaps he cannot see that other city, he cannot answer the calls we are getting and meet with the groups we are meeting with. He will not take the time to visit the senior citizens who might have $100 of discretionary income. He does not have a sense of what it means to be a senior citizen on a fixed income, an income now endangered by what the Government announced in this Budget. He does not see that other city, yet it is there. You can see it in the long line-ups at food kitchens and food banks. You can see it in the increasing number of shelters.

With the announcement of this federal Budget, we are changing the rules of the game after the game has started.
The message has fallen on the deaf ears of the Government. The first or second Member on that side to get up and respond to this motion talked about fairness, honesty and how the opposition was failing in both areas. I challenge that Member to show me the fairness and honesty of this Budget, specifically the proposal advocating partial deindexation of Old Age Security pensions.
Borrowing Authority Act
Where is the fairness, honesty and integrity of that proposal? Members opposite have a short memory. They fail to remember that several months ago they all fanned out across this country and said they would not touch the pensions of our senior citizens. They would not ask those people to bear the burden of the economic price we have to pay. A sacred trust, is what the Prime Minister said. After a few months in power, one of the first things in the Budget, one of the first Tory documents to be presented in this House, reneges on that very fundamental and clearly articulated promise to senior citizens. The Minister of National Health and Welfare, in answer to a question I posed, said we have no option, no alternative, but he did and he knows it.
Where is the fairness in a Budget proposal which means that a household with two children earning $15,000 to $20,000 a year will have to pay 36 per cent more in taxes by 1990, but a family earning $200,000 is looking at a 2 per cent increase? Where is the fairness and integrity there? There is none. Where is the fairness in the capital gains tax bonanza? The Government says it will affect everyone, small businesses all across the country, but one only has to look at the 1983 statistics concerning capital gains taxes to see that almost 70 per cent of those claiming capital gains represent only 4 per cent of the Canadian population.
We on this side of the House and seniors of this country ask ourselves: What about the other 96 per cent? The Hon. Member across the way said we have to pay our bills. We have to pay the bankers because they will not wait. That, Mr. Chairman, is the mentality we are attempting to fight, a mentality which suggests we have to pay our bills and let other people suffer. The senior citizens have bills to pay, too. We are trying to send a message to the Government that if it can easily, arbitrarily and regressively undermine the seniors' pensions, then it ought to be prepared to swallow the same pill on the same day, and that day is today, but the Government is not prepared to do so. It is not prepared to make that sacrifice or accept the same punishment it has inflicted on the senior citizens.
The first reaction of the Government was that this motion would further hurt the poor and disadvantaged of this country because it assumes that if the Government was to reduce its spending by 3 per cent, that is the constituency it would cut the 3 per cent of spending from. Well, that perhaps says more than does our motion. That message to senior citizens is perhaps even stronger than our message to the Government. We understand the message we are getting from the Government, we understand the mind-set of Members opposite. We understand their philosophical bent and it is unfortunate, but it clearly delineates their side from this side.
We are having a rally next Tuesday in Toronto at 12 noon in Nathan Phillips Square. Once again we are getting a magnificent response from senior citizens' organizations. We have invited members of the Government, the Prime Minister and the Minister of National Health and Welfare to attend because it is important to speak to those seniors who will be affected by this clause. This rally is not being organized on a

Borrowing Authority Act
political partisan basis because no one in the House has a monopoly on concerns facing senior citizens or concerns facing the poor and disabled. We have the responsibility to speak for those groups and bring their concerns to the attention of the Government.
We want the Prime Minister to come to that rally because he will see something very different than what he saw in Quebec yesterday. This event will be much more spontaneous and real than what happened in Quebec because he will see the look of desperation on the faces of those individuals who come to him. It will be difficult for him to defend the indefensible in front of those individuals. If he takes the time to listen to those concerns and anxieties facing those senior citizens, he will not hesitate to reverse this regressive move he instigated several weeks ago in the Budget.
We are trying to speak for the aspirations of those people. Another Member opposite talked about democracy and how we were somehow undemocratic. He suggested that we are being obstructionist and overreacting to this concern. He ought not to teach us about democracy and profess to be democratic.
The senior citizens of this country have rallied daily for the last two weeks in an attempt to send the message to Government that it is wrong. The business community and business organizations of this country have also rallied and tried to send that message to the Government. The municipal Governments throughout the country are passing resolutions in their council chambers, regardless of the fact that this is a federal issue, in order to send a message to the Government that its measure is wrong. The provincial Governments are doing the same thing. We have witnessed Tory premiers and Tory Governments, and provincial governments in Manitoba and Quebec sending that message, despite the fact that it is a federal issue.
The Official Opposition and the NDP are raising this matter daily in Question Period and in debate, as we are this morning. If the Hon. Member wants to talk about democracy, he should not ignore the message that has been coming from the legislative groups in the last two weeks.
Members opposite cannot spend the summer in the belief that this issue will have disappeared by September 15. This issue will not die, not because the Opposition Parties will not let it die, but because Canadians from one coast to the other will not let it die. Canadians, particularly elderly Canadians, are saying that this issue is fundamental to their existence-to the social contract that they have with this state. As Canadians, they are entitled to Old Age Security pensions and to the full indexation of those pensions. This social contract is part of being Canadian. It is not acceptable to change the rules after someone has paid into that pension in order to plan their future after the age of 65 and collect a certain amount of money.
The Government argues that this measure will help future generations and provide money for future pensioners. What about those people who are 65, 75 and 85 today? Who is speaking for those individuals? Who is speaking for today's
pensioners who want the obligations of that social contract to be respected and honoured? We on this side are fighting for that obligation and we are not afraid to speak for those individuals because they need representation.
We are sending a message, through this simple motion, that the Government has not listened and has not reacted well. Once again, we call upon its sense of compassion, fair play and morality to come clean and admit that this regressive policy to deindex is wrong and unfair. We call upon the Government to show leadership by saying it is prepared to restore full indexing as a commitment to our senior citizens.

Mr. Chairman, I join this debate because of the importance I associate with its substance and that I believe the effects of these regressive measures that were contained in the Budget will have a long lasting effect on many Canadians.
It should be noted that the debate was touched off by the Honourable-I use the word with great care-House leader for the Government. He made some very uncomplimentary remarks with regard to Opposition Members. I do not believe that he was questioning their motive, however it could be argued that perhaps he was. I believe that the House Leader said some very unfair and uncomplimentary things about Members of the Opposition relating to this particular debate.
What that Hon. Member has failed to recognize is that the Liberal Party of Canada is standing behind this issue in an attempt to have full indexation restored to our senior citizens. However, along with the Liberal Party of Canada are other individuals, groups and organizations who believe that our cause is just, fair and equitable on behalf of senior citizens in Canada.
I would be remiss if I did not take this opportunity to share with the House what some of those other individuals have said and who they are. There is no secret that the Premier of the Province of Prince Edward Island is against the deindexation of Old Age Security. Is the House Leader of the Conservative Party suggesting to Members of the House and Canadians that because some object so vigorously that somehow they are undemocratic, appalling, unfair and not carrying out their tasks as elected representatives?
The Premier of Newfoundland is also on the record publicly and within his own province as being opposed to this very regressive measure. Of course, the Premier of the Province of Nova Scotia has said very clearly in Nova Scotia and elsewhere in Atlantic Canada that he and his Party are against the deindexation of Old Age Security.
However, the list does not stop with political leaders. It includes the business community. The list includes senior citizens' organizations and non-profit organizations which have issued news releases and held press conferences to cast shame upon the Government of Canada for introducing such regressive measures. We all know that the government caucus meeting held on Saturday-

What do you know about it?

I know exactly what went on, and I know exactly what will take place. We know that the Government will change this measure and restore full indexation. However, the question becomes: "When will the Government do it?" The issue which senior citizens find so distasteful is that the Prime Minister has not lived up to his clear and unequivocal commitment in the Province of Quebec in July, 1984. That commitment has been replayed time and time again and showed very clearly that the Prime Minister would restore, according to his own words, full indexation.
However, several months later, we found that the Minister of Finance went against his Prime Minister and introduced a budget measure which flew in the face of that commitment. Senior citizens find that to be particularly distasteful. They believed their Prime Minister, rightly or wrongly, depending upon one's political persuasion. They believed that their Prime Minister would restore full indexation, only to discover, as was suggested by one of his own constituents-and I use the words of that constituent-that they have been "lied" to. It is unparliamentary for me to use that word, and I will not use it, but that is what was said by a Canadian residing in the riding of the Right Hon. Prime Minister. That comment ought to be taken seriously, not only for the tone in which the constituent said it, but for the substance of what he was saying.
It is fine and dandy for Members of Parliament, regardless of their political association, who earn in excess of $70,000- and some earn substantially more-to say that that may not be so devastating. However, senior citizens on a fixed income have to make plans, have to budget for their expenditures and revenues. When they are faced, out of the clear blue sky, with cut-backs in the money anticipated to meet their expenditures, that is devastating. Perhaps it is not so for Members of Parliament, but to senior citizens, after working hard for 35 years or 40 years raising their families, it can be a devastating and appalling feature of their economic viability as citizens. The principle is rooted deeply. I appeal to the sense of fairness of Hon. Members opposite. It may mean that a senior citizen will be overdue in paying the telephone bill. It may mean that a taxi cannot be taken to go to the hospital to visit a loved one. It may be that extra little bit which a senior citizen gives to a neighbourhood boy to go to the store to buy a few groceries during inclement weather. Surely those of us who sit in this awesome Chamber, the distinction that it is, realize that the Minister of Finance cannot stand in his place and say to Canadians: "Bravo, I have done the right thing".
What toughness is there in taking money from senior citizens? I say to the Hon. Member from Halifax and to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development that the Minister should have been tough on those who could afford it, and I refer to the capital gains provisions in the Budget. In my view, that would have been cause for Hon. Members on all sides of the House to stand in their places and say: "Yes, the Minister of Finance is standing up to those who can most afford to sacrifice". However, what has happened has been the complete opposite. The Minister of Finance and the Prime
Borrowing Authority Act
Minister have broken their commitments to the elderly of Canada.
Mr. Chairman, you know, as a distinguished Member of the House, that 1.7 million Canadian senior citizens live below the poverty line. I ask Hon. Members on all sides: Where is the toughness in saying to senior citizens living below the poverty line that they will receive less? In my view, the Minister of Finance has committed a major political blunder. Of course that happens, but it is important what one does to recover from a political blunder. I suggest to the Minister of Finance and Hon. Members who support him and believe in his sincerity and his policies, that they have to stand and be counted to have this regressive measure changed, changed to honour the commitment of the Prime Minister in July 1984.
In terms of the capital gains provisions, is it tough to say to the wealthy of the country that they will be given $300 million this year and $600 million in the next fiscal year? Is it tough to say to them that Canadian taxpayers will give them $1.2 billion by 1990? Is that toughness or, as some senior citizens have said, is that copping out?
This measure calls upon the most vulnerable segment of Canadian society. It calls upon them, after years of sacrifice, whether it was during the First World War or the Second World War. It calls upon them after years of productive life, trying to build their communities, to strengthen the educational system and to build churches so that Canadians would have an opportunity to worship the God of their choice. Now, in their years of retirement and reflection, this regressive measure is calling upon them to make a financial contribution. That is not fair in anyone's eyes.
Members of Parliament, particularly Members of the Government, must accept that this was a political blunder. They have an obligation today to end the uncertainty with which senior citizens have been confronted since the announcement of the Budget on May 23, 1985. For the edification of all Canadians, I must emphasize that uncertainty of Canadians on a Fixed income is a major reason for frustration and worry.
The fairness of this Budget does not lie with the senior citizens of Canada. They have been treated unfairly. When will this unfairness stop? The Government will have an opportunity today or tomorrow to end the unfairness of this regressive tax measure. Some political commentators would say that it would not show toughness if the Government backed down and that it should stick to its guns. However, that is not what Governments are elected to do. Governments are not elected to appease those who sit in the press gallery. Governments are elected to serve the best interests of the people. Government Members can take satisfaction in changing this regressive tax measure in that they will be doing the right thing on behalf of all Canadians. So what if there are a few editorials in the newspapers condemning the Government for backtracking? In my view it must.
I sincerely ask Government Members to stand in their places and right this wrong. If the wrong continues to affect

Borrowing Authority Act
senior citizens in any province of Canada, the issue will become so great that it will become virtually impossible for the Government of Canada to back down. To continue with this unfair measure will cause strife and worry for a population which deserves much better. This ought not to be a political issue and it ought not be debated on the floor of the House of Commons because it is a wrong. Each of us should stand in our place and vote today to right this wrong for the benefit of the senior citizens of our country. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in participating in the debate on this amendment, I would like to give the most visible message possible. This pile of paper contains over 2,000 names of senior citizens from the City of Winnipeg. That is only a small percentage of the number of people in that city who are deeply protesting the action of the Government.
Over the weekend I read the statements of the Hon. Member for St. Boniface who said he did not think this was much of an issue because he had only had four or five phone calls on it. I looked at the addresses on these petitions and saw Provencher Boulevard, Dumoulin Street, Goulet Street and Marion Street. Hundreds of people from that Member's riding have signed these petitions. I bring that to the attention of the House because it highlights what is very much at stake in this debate. What is important is not only the substance of the action taken by the Government, but the way it has handled this matter and broken its trust with the Canadian people.
The Prime Minister has more gyrations than a run-away corkscrew. We do not know from one day to the next what turn, twist, zig, or zag he will be taking. Let us look at the record on old age pensions and support. During the election campaign we heard the famous declaration of the sacred trust with strong hints that support to senior citizens would be improved. That was good during the election campaign, but after the election we began to hear some murmurings from the Minister of Finance that the Government was going to reexamine the universality of the pension scheme. It was no longer sacred, they were beginning to review the matter.
When questions were raised in the House of Commons and elsewhere in the country, the Prime Minister jumped back on the bandwagon saying that the incomes of senior citizens would not be touched because they were essential. In the dark of the night, the Minister of National Health and Welfare redrafted his Green Paper or White Paper in order to change the matter. That paper said that in the re-examination of social programs there would be no reduction in the income support for senior citizens. That was another turn in the road.
Then it was Budget time and we saw a whole series of actions that have substantially undermined the income position of older people in the country. We have heard the argument for deindexation many times. In the next four years, individual senior citizens will have a decreased buying power of $1,500 in today's dollars. Furthermore, the problem is compounded by the substantial increase in sales taxes on basic commodities, a
regressive form of taxation which is to be applied to detergent supplies, candy and pet food. An old saying by W. C. Fields goes that anyone who hates children and dogs can't be all bad. The Conservative Government is making that particular axiom real. I suppose W. C. Fields helped to write the Budget. There must have been some source for that.
The fact of the matter is that the Government has substantially reduced in a regressive way the purchasing power of senior citizens. Not only has their direct income support been taken away, but their purchasing power has been taken away. As if that were not enough, a third whammy is added through reductions in transfer payments to the provinces by $2 billion between now and 1990. This can only mean that there will be either a substantial reduction in health services or increased taxation or user-fees at the provincial level. Compounding that, the municipalities that also supply specialized services for senior citizens like day care centres and transportation will also have to raise taxes or cut back on programs. The Budget is clearly a multifaceted attack on the income base of senior citizens.
When the Budget was first brought down, we rose in the House to ask the Government why it was doing this. Let us think of the interesting sequence of arguments that have been used since that time. First, government Members said that senior citizens wanted them to do that and were all supporting them. The Minister of National Health and Welfare said that he talked to all kinds of senior citizens who wanted the Government to reduce the deficit and take away their incomes. However, when challenged, he could not name one individual or group that had said that to him. That argument did not fly very well.

June 18, 1985

What was it that the Prime Minister said the other week after he had been leader of the Party for two years? Oh, yes, he said that the press has been hurtful to him.
