speechtext:
The fact of the matter is that that is far less than what the Prime Minister is spending on his office. This issue carries with it not only the serious and incredible damage being done to millions upon millions of Canadians, but also brings into clear focus the incredible and almost unbelieveable way in which the Conservative Government has acquired divine right in a matter of nine months. It does not have to listen to the people. All those protestations about consultations, building consensus and working with the public are being totally disregarded.
What is the purpose? What are government Members trying to achieve with this? It would be different if they said that this Budget would somehow achieve something worth while. We would not agree with them, but their argument now is that
Borrowing Authority Act
somehow this sacrifice that only the senior citizens and lower income families are going to have to make will result in some great economic millennium. However, the Government's own Budget denies that in its descriptions.
Government Members are talking about a growth rate that is less than 50 per cent of the growth rate over the past two years. The fallacy in their economic thinking is that somehow the Government can withdraw close to $40 billion worth of purchasing power from the economy over the next four years, yet they assume that the demand for consumer goods, housing and services will continue. Regardless of how many tax giveaways and breaks are given to the investor community and regardless of how happy the friends of the Minister of Finance on the Toronto Stock Exchange are, if there is not a basic economic demand, business will not expand to meet it. Businesses expand to meet consumer demand. However, if people do not have money because it has been taken away from them by enormous tax grabs, business will not expand.
The Wall Street Journal has said that this is economic suicide. The Government is not putting money back into the economy. It is not stimulating consumer demand. Instead, it is reducing and withdrawing money from circulation and there will, therefore, be far less stimulus and far less incentive.
Since this does not make economic sense, we have to ask what government Members are doing. It has become very clear that the close to $3.5 billion that is being taken away from senior citizens and the billions of dollars that are being taken away from low-income families have nothing to do with reducing the deficit. The sales taxes and deindexation can be matched up with the give-aways through the capital gains program, the cancellation of the PGRT and the other forms of tax offerings to a very select, privileged group in this country. Because of that, this is a Government that is prepared to have millions of Canadians pay for the benefits that will go to less than 4 per cent of the population.
The only economic sense which one could draw from that is that it is the Government's fundamental belief that economic growth and stimulus will come from the privileged elite. It will come from catering and servicing that particular restricted, hothouse group of Canadians. The Government believes that if there are a few crumbs which trickle off the table to ordinary Canadians, then that is fine. The old trickle-down theory was discounted back in the 1920s when we put social Darwinism to bed. It was the rule of the economic jungle, which had been the prevailing notions up to that period, which was placed in the storehouse of worn-out ideas forever. It took 1985 and the Prime Minister to bring back the time-worn idea that aid to the privileged would result in benefits to all.
I think Canadian people are wising up to what has taken place in the Budget. They are beginning to realize that the net impact will not be for the benefit of young families who want to buy homes, workers who want to be retrained, or older people who want to maintain their income security. The Government is helping a small circle of individuals. The rest is

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
based on some faith that those individuals will generate a massive wave of growth and that we will all rise the tide.
It is a very precarious and dangerous economic theory. It is no wonder the Minister of Finance is leaving the country today and not returning until Parliament recesses. It is no wonder he thinks that the best refuge is about 5,000 miles away. He is recognizing that the underlying foundations of the Budget are built on shifting sands which are being badly eroded day by day. The only way in which he can save face is to get out of the country. He is once again, as we have seen since the Government took office, evading responsibility for taking the tough and right decisions. He and the Prime Minister think they can get by with fancy tricks, public opinion polls and public relations gimmicks. Once again they are trying to replace solid and tough economic decisions with coloured lights and cosmetics.
This Government does not like to govern. It does not know how to govern and it does not want to govern. It does not want to make the kind of decisions which are necessary. The Government has now been abandoned by all of its friends and allies. The business community has said: "Don't do it". Provincial Premiers, many of whom are Tories, have said: "Don't do it". Many articulate and well-informed social organizations have said: "Don't do it". Can the Government name one organization, aside from the Riverdale Conservative Association, which thinks that the Government should do it? Is it able to provide any evidence that there is overwhelming support for the budget measures? It says that it has the Decima poll. I am sorry, I will correct my remarks. Allan Gregg says that the Government should do it. If that is the basis on which policy is being decided and consensus is being formed, I wish the Government would tell us that.
With seer wisdom and the prophet of forecasting, the Conservative Party has decreed that it is okay. All the protest of individual senior groups and the abandonment of the Government's business allies does not convince the Government and the caucus. We have brought forward the amendment for that very reason. We believe there are Conservative Members of Parliament who understand their constituencies and who are not prepared to buy the blarney of the Prime Minister. We believe they are willing to represent what they know is of deep, abiding and crucial concern to their constituents.
The amendment will give the Government time to convene and examine its actions. Obviously the weekend was a flop. However, it is not too late as there are still two weeks left in the session. We are asking the Government to take a look at what it is doing. It should honestly examine what kind of impact it will have on people. The Government should ask itself if this is really what it wants to achieve. Does it really want to tell seniors and young families that it is prepared to withdraw their incomes for the sake of a small boom on the Toronto Stock Exchange? Is that the trade-off which the Government is presenting to Canadians?
We hope that the wisdom and the judgment which exists in the caucus will ultimately prevail and that the Prime Minister,
in his last zig and zag, will make the right decision, which all Canadians want him to make.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I listened with a great deal of interest to the comments which were made by my colleague from Winnipeg-Fort Garry. His comments prompt me to raise a couple of issues which have come to mind during the last two or three days when I have listened to the exchanges which have taken place in the House over the deindexing issue.
Last Sunday morning I spent some time wandering around my constituency talking to people, as I do almost every Sunday morning. I went to the local doughnut shop and chatted with people who like to bring me up to date on the events, as they see them, in Parliament and in the area. The question which was raised most often was the question of the Government's action with respect to the deindexing of pensions. It struck me as passing strange, because many of those people were not on pensions.
The same morning I read in The Saturday Star or The Sunday Star about a number of Conservative back-benchers who had indicated that they had not received an overwhelming amount of representation on that particular issue. Many Conservative Members seemed to feel that it was not an issue of great importance in the minds of their constituents. They were not receiving large volumes of letters and they were not being stopped on the street. Their telephones in their offices were not being rung off the hook by those who were desirous of expressing their individual concerns. I was puzzled about that. I wondered why it was that everyone whom I met on the streets of Hamilton, on the Sparks Street Mall, or walking out of my apartment building in Ottawa asked me about the question of deindexing, or at least made reference to it. Why was it that 1 was receiving those kind of representations? Why were my colleagues in the New Democratic Party receiving those kind of representations? Why were Members of the Liberal Party receiving these representations? Yet apparently the Tory backbenchers were not.
I say this in all kindness, but for some Tory back-benchers it may be simply because of inexperience. They perhaps have not been involved in politics for very long and do not have a routine established for allowing people access to them. Those Members of the Conservative Party who are here at the moment and who have gone through a number of election campaigns could perhaps cast their minds back to election campaigns when they did not receive the kind of support they had anticipated. Perhaps they noticed that people did not talk to them in anger, that some people, particularly elderly people, did not talk to them at all. I find that as a rule when people are upset with their Member of Parliament during an election campaign-except for the few who know you reasonably well-they do not tell you how angry they are. They simply leave you alone. They talk to each other, but they do not confront you because they have decided they are not going to support what you are doing. So for those Members of the Government who perhaps wonder why they are not getting the
June 18, 1985

kind of response we in the Opposition are getting, that may well be part of the answer.
Perhaps in the past people would have raised an issue with their Member of Parliament in passing because they were not directly involved and, therefore, did not feel embarrassed about making their case. They may not feel comfortable making a case on their own behalf on an issue such as this. I would urge Members of the Government to not assume automatically that because they are not inundated with phone calls and correspondence, it is indicative of complacency. I suspect it could well be indicative of a sense of frustration and acute embarrassment that many old people feel over an issue which touches them directly, which affects their very day to day lives and which will undermine their income capacity.
I ask Members of the Liberal Party if they found during the last election campaign that people simply did not talk to them on the doorsteps because they were not voting for the Liberal Party this time? I found in past elections that they simply say, thank you very much, take the leaflet and walk away. They don't really want to confront you. I think that could well be the reason why Members of the Government are not receiving the kind of response which the rest of us in the House of Commons are receiving over this issue.
In addition to that, quite clearly those who are most affected align themselves with those who are raising these concerns. It is not unnatural that people who feel their future undermined by the proposal of the Government would, out of necessity, align themselves with Members of Parliament who are raising the issue. Given the fact that there is no indication as yet, other than a few individual instances, that any Members of the Government are about to stand up and be counted in opposition to this rather harsh measure, I would think that that would be a good reason why a large number of people are not yet making contact with them in an effort to try to get this matter reviewed by the Government.
Having said that, I want to now turn to what I consider to be the nub of the issue. It really goes to the heart of the beliefs of the present Minister of Finance. For years the Minister of Finance has believed that universality is a bad thing. He has for years believed that there could be some way devised to, as he puts it, get more money to the poor while not providing so much for the rich. He has spoken frequently about the need to reconsider universality as an integral part of social programs in Canada.
This is the first substantive assault on universality. The Minister of Finance raised the matter last November, perhaps foolishly, and the Prime Minister, after having suffered some abuse as a result of the Minister of Finance having raised the question of universality, beat him over the head and forced him to withdraw. That was the first step since the Government took office in September toward achieving what the Minister of Finance has been saying he believes in for many years. That was, of course, followed by this measure which the Government tells us is intended to reduce the deficit. It is the seniors' contribution to the deficit reduction program of the Government and it will raise some $250 million.
Borrowing Authority Act
Given that we know the income levels of the overwhelming majority of senior citizens in Canada are barely above the poverty line, it does not make much sense to ask those who have so little to make such a contribution. It makes even less sense when we view it in the context of all of the Government's expenditures and all of the other areas where Government might turn in order to find an alternative way of raising $250 million.
Rather than be simply critical, the NDP Party sat down and looked at the various ways in which Government might raise the $250 million it requires. We offered, as you will recall, Mr. Chairman, five ways. I am prepared to concede that they are not the only ways and it is entirely possible to come up with an additional 15 or 20 ways, and perhaps even more. These five ways may not, in the minds of the Conservative Party, be the most appropriate ways, but they are concrete ways which could be used by the Government to raise the $250 million which it proposes to raise from the partial deindexing of the pensions of our senior citizens.
When we think about senior citizens, without going any farther, we have to think that these are the very people who built the society we are now enjoying. These are the people who worked the long torturous hours, who worked under unsafe working conditions, who worked in plants which paid little in way of remuneration, who worked without adequate vacations and who had very little opportunity to save for their retirement. These people in many cases went through the Depression and may have lost everything they owned in the 1930s. They went to war on behalf of Canada and, in the final analysis, they put together for us this society we enjoy. We are now saying to them, "While you did make those sacrifices and they were important, and, by God, we are grateful, we are not grateful enough to index your pension to the cost of living". We are grateful enough to index it to anything over 3 per cent of the cost of living. We have to raise $250 million and notwithstanding our gratitude, that $250 million is more important than our sense of what we owe to our senior citizens for what they have done for us.
We said, let's take a look at the options. We offered a number, and I do not intend to go back over them again, but I want to suggest that there is one which appeals to me and I do not quite understand, even yet, why it does not make sense. 1 would love to hear someone on the Conservative front benches attempt to explain to me why we should go out and borrow money in order to offset the money we do not now collect from the corporate sector, money which they owe. Why should we ask seniors and others to increase their tax burden in order to say to a very lucrative corporate sector that they can defer paying their taxes indefinitely? Why do we not require from those who are allowed to defer their taxes that at the very least they pay to the Government of Canada the interest charges that the Government incurs in borrowing the money they would be required to pay if they were not allowed to defer it?

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
I say to my. hon. friend from Bow River: does that not make sense when you think about it? If I have to go out and borrow money in order to replenish the coffers because I do not collect from the corporate sector the money they owe, then the very least I could expect from them would be that they pay the interest on the money I borrowed. Do you agree with that? Surely you have to think that makes a little bit of sense.
Do you know that if we simply charge a rate of 10 per cent, which is below the rate they could borrow in the market-place, we could collect on an annual basis some $3 billion. Why should they not be prepared to make that kind of contribution rather than ask the senior citizens to do without the indexing provision for pensions which are already woefully inadequate? 1 look around and I ask if there is anyone on either side of the House, even you, Mr. Chairman, who will stand up and tell me why. I mean, is there something wrong with the logic I am offering? Can anyone tell me that there is something wrong with suggesting that it is better that the corporate sector pay interest on the money it owes rather than collect $250 million from the senior citizens? That is the question. Does the Hon. Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development want to rise and answer? I would be pleased to sit and listen. No, I see him shrinking back into his seat again and I can understand why. He is a sensitive man. He is the kind of individual I anticipate would be fighting in caucus and Cabinet to advance the kind of suggestion we have put forward.
I say to you, Mr. Chairman, that with that one measure alone we would collect $3 billion and it would more than offset the $250 million we intend to take from the seniors. That would leave us with $2.75 billion to do with whatever we pleased. If you really only need the $250 million, instead of charging 10 per cent, charge 3 per cent or 2.5 per cent if that would make you happy. By doing that you will raise exactly what you need. I say to my colleague from Hamilton East, who is no doubt about to rise and support the position I am putting forward, that quite clearly any person sitting here or watching or reading or hearing about it later on will come to the inevitable conclusion that what we are asking for is eminently sensible. It is irrefutable in its logic. It will work absolutely no hardship on the corporate sector. It will relieve us of the necessity, if there is indeed a necessity, of turning to the seniors for that money. It will enable us to act responsibly toward the people on whose backs this country was built.
I could go on, Mr. Chairman. I could outline the other four proposals which, when added together, would make for many billions of dollars which could be used to offset the deficit and provide better programs. We could debate the later. However, quite clearly, the Government seems to have become deaf not only to the logic of my argument but also to the pleas of senior citizens and young people, as well as deaf to the pleas of the Premiers of the Provinces.
It seems the Government does not want to lose face. I want to tell you, Mr. Chairman, that if it were me, if I were the Minister of Finance or if I were the Prime Minister and I had inadvertently allowed a proposal like this to come forward in my name and had then the benefit of reviewing it and seeing
the consequences of my action, I would rise in my place and say I have made a mistake and I am going to change it. That is what we are asking the Prime Minister to do.

Mr. Chairman, indeed I would like to join my voice to that of the Hon. Member for Hamilton Mountain who has spoken to the very heart of the issue we are discussing today. I happened to be here in the House this morning when the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate moved an amemd-nent which said that the Government was asking the Parliament of Canada to approve a motion which would allow it to borrow billions of dollars at the same time it is putting a 3 per cent squeeze on senior citizens' pensions, the very people in our society who can least afford to pay. Given that, we then say to the Government we want to reduce its borrowing authority by a corresponding 3 per cent. The Minister of Finance tells the senior citizens to cut back on their bus fare, food and hydro bills by 3 per cent. Well, we called upon the Government to cut back by 3 per cent, and what was the response of Government spokesmen? The Government House Leader, upon hearing the Liberal amendment, immediately rose in his place and said that means we are going to cut back further on the senior citizens. That means we are going to decrease senior citizens' pensions by another 3 per cent. That seems to me to be indicative of the kind of knee-jerk reaction of this Government. The Government House Leader, confronted with the amendment put by the Liberal opposition, stands in his place and says we will carry out those cuts on the backs of the seniors. That is the mentality of this Government.
I hope I will have a chance to carry on after Question Period on this very important issue, Mr. Chairman.

speechtext:

June 18, 1985

subtopic: SOUTH AFRICA-DEMAND FOR RECALL OF CANADIAN AMBASSADOR
SOUTH AFRICA-DEMAND FOR RECALL OF CANADIAN AMBASSADOR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, last week South Africa's stormtroopers swooped into Botswana under cover of darkness, shooting 16 men, women, and children, and blowing up the houses of black refugees.
Sunday, the fury of reincarnated Nazism was again unleashed, this time upon 5,000 churchgoers in Soweto whose singular crime was to have gathered in commemoration of the victims of the Soweto massacre nine years ago.
In response to the Botswana raid, the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) said Canada deplores violence from any quarter, thus implying that the victims share an equivalent measure of guilt, while politely requesting South Africa to respect the sovereignty and independence of its neighbours.
Even the U.S. administration, which regards South Africa somewhat sympathetically as a bulwark against Communism, has recalled its ambassador to South Africa.
Will the Government again turn a blind eye even while a member of its own diplomatic corps is gassed in church, or will it immediately recall its ambassador as a sign of the revulsion of the Canadian people at this racist, outlaw regime, and act immediately to implement economic sanctions against South Africa?

subtopic: PROTECTION SOUGHT FOR NIAGARA GRAPE LANDS
PROTECTION SOUGHT FOR NIAGARA GRAPE LANDS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the 44,000 acres of tender fruit and grape lands left in Niagara is a resource under attack. They are unique. There is no other combination of quality soils and climate like them anywhere
else in Canada. There are few lands of this quality anywhere else in the world. Still, the growers must have a reasonable return in keeping with their investment and cost of operations.
Peach growing declined when the processing end of the industry was hit by offshore competition. The home market was flooded and subjected to a deliberate attack to put that industry out of business. Those peach orchards were converted to grape vineyards.
High quality grapes are being grown for quality wine. But, unhappily, those grape growers and wine producers are caught in the same type of squeeze that forced the peach growers out of business. Unless the problem of dumping of offshore import wines is resolved soon, the wine industry will be placed in jeopardy. We can make trade a two-way street, providing an export market for our wines, or we can protect the domestic market from dumping.
If those growers cannot make a reasonable return, cannot make a living from the sweat of their labour, then these acres will go the way of so many others-urban development. The fate of these lands is in the hands of the Government.

subtopic: BENEFITS ACCRUING TO NORTHERN ONTARIO FROM FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT
BENEFITS ACCRUING TO NORTHERN ONTARIO FROM FEDERAL-PROVINCIAL AGREEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on Friday, June 14, a very significant event took place in the town of Kirkland Lake in my riding of Timiskaming. The federal Minister of State for Mines (Mr. Layton) and the provincial Minister of Natural Resources jointly announced a five-year, $30 million federal-provincial mineral development agreement. The signing of this agreement is truly symbolic of the co-operation that now exists between the federal and provincial Governments.
Under this subagreement to the Canada-Ontario Economic and Regional Development Agreement, a road which was proposed for construction back in 1928 has finally come about, and I congratulate the pioneers-the prospectors and the developers-who fought so long and hard for this access road. Once again it shows that the Government that was elected last September 4 knows and understands Canadians.
The construction of this access road to mining areas in northern Ontario will bring great prosperity to my riding. Employment opportunities will flourish in the forestry, tourism, and mining sectors of Timiskaming.
The signing of this agreement demonstrates once again my Government's commitment to creating jobs for Canadians.

June 18, 1985

subtopic: AWARDING OF GRANT TO WINNIPEG INTERNATIONAL CENTRE
AWARDING OF GRANT TO WINNIPEG INTERNATIONAL CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to bring to the attention of the Chamber a storm that is brewing in Winnipeg over the awarding of a $29,900 grant by the Minister of State for Multiculturalism (Mr. Murta) to the International Centre.
Members of the Centre and of the ethno cultural community are outraged over the circumstances surrounding the grant. First, Mr. Tom Denton, the sponsor of the application and a former PC candidate, signed as the treasurer of the Centre's multicultural committee. In truth, though, the committee was unaware of his application, and there is no position of treasurer. Second, four individuals listed as sponsors on the form did not know or approve of their names being used to obtain the federal moneys. Third, the grant application was for $28,400, but was approved in the amount of $29,900. Fourth, the application was not dated and, finally, while the public is being told it will support a one-year project, the grant indicated the period was only from January to May. Therefore, has the money been spent and, if not, will it be returned since the deadline has already come and gone?
Members of the Centre and the community have written to the Auditor General and the Minister of State for Multiculturalism asking for an immediate investigation into these improprieties and the appearance of a quick grab for some patronage dollars. I, too, call on the Minister to investigate these serious shortcomings and urge him to clear the air quickly.

subtopic: VISITS BY UNITED STATES SUBMARINES TO WEST COAST PORTS
VISITS BY UNITED STATES SUBMARINES TO WEST COAST PORTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, Los Angeles and Sturgeon class submarines, which are being equipped with sea launched Cruise missiles known as Tomahawks, have visited Nanoose Bay and Esquimalt Harbour in the last few days.
Nuclear equipped Tomahawks have a range of 1,500 miles, and a 200 kilotonne warhead. The American Navy Director of Strategic and Theatre Nuclear Warfare said:
The increased strike range of a large number of surface platforms operating under carrier air cover and independent, covert, forward deployed submarines presents the Soviets a formidable threat.
Not only are the Soviets threatened by these Tomahawk missiles, our entire world is threatened.
Were the Los Angeles and Sturgeon submarines that came into Nanoose and Esquimalt nuclear armed? We do not know. The United States will neither confirm nor deny, and the Canadian Government is afraid to ask. In the absence of such information, New Zealand had enough gumption to refuse access to all American warships. Canada should take the same step.
The Canada-U.S. Agreement for the submarine base at Nanoose expires in April, 1986. This agreement has not contributed to world peace or to Canadian security. It should not be renewed.

subtopic: SUPPORT FOR CONTENTS
SUPPORT FOR CONTENTS

CONSTRUCTION OF TOXICOLOGY RESEARCH CENTRE AT UNIVERSITY OF SASKATCHEWAN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 am pleased to advise the House of a major development concerning environmental research in Canada. Since October I have worked with the Minister of the Environment (Mrs. Blais-Grenier), the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Wise), the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean), and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Epp), to promote the much needed Toxicology Research Centre at the University of Saskatchewan. This university was identified by the National Research Council as one of three centres to undertake toxicological research in Canada.
I am also pleased to advise the House that, through a $2 million grant from the Centres of Specialization of the Secretary of State, Phase 1 of construction of the Toxicology Research Centre will commence this year. This Centre will be supported by the faculties of Health Sciences, Veterinary Medicine, Pharmacy, Chemistry, Biology, and Agriculture. In addition, the Wildlife Services Division of the Department of the Environment and the private sector will utilize the facility.
June 18, 1985

The Toxicology Research Centre will serve all of western Canada and conduct environmental research of critical importance to all of Canada. Adequate funding for the entire Centre is not in place. It is hoped that the remainder of the funding will be made available as resources from the federal and provincial Governments, the university, and the private sector, permit.
All Hon. Members of the House should applaud the federal Government and the University of Saskatchewan for recognizing the importance of toxicological research and making a strong commitment which will ensure a safer environment for our children and generations to come.

It will be many years before Canadians, through both Parliament and the courts, begin to have a rough idea of what their society will be like with the inception of the new Charter.

Equality will eventually be defined in a way which reflects the values, beliefs, and convictions of individual Canadians.
Toward this goal the Secretary of State (Mr. McLean) provides grants for women's organizations attemp ing to bring meaning, in different ways, to the concept of equality in the Canadian context.

It is a wholesale violation of the principles of the Charter if a specific feminist view is imposed and encouraged to the exclusion of alternatives from thousands of other Canadian women.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, it is indeed a great week, not only for the City of Ottawa and for Parliament, but also for the whole of Canada in that two distinguished parliamentarians are celebrating their birthdays, the Hon. Stanley Knowles, who was honoured in the House today on his seventh-seventh birthday, and the Hon. Jack Pickersgill, who is eighty. In fact, both these gentlemen gave much to Canada in Parliament and outside. It seems to me that when we are discussing the punitive measures which have been put forward by the Government toward senior citizens, we should start looking at the work and the contribution of people like Stanley Knowles and Jack Pickersgill. Many people in Canada did not have the opportunity to sit in Parliament. Many people in Canada did not have the same opportunity as Members of Parliament who now sit in the House to accrue pension benefits. There are

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
many senior citizens in the Province of Ontario, and we know that 40 per cent of our senior citizens are living below the poverty line.
What has been the response of the Minister of Finance? Day after day, hour after hour, he talks about deficit reduction and job creation in the House of Commons. I do not think we are asking Stanley Knowles to get out on the job market again. I do not think that Jack Pickersgill should be forced into the employment sector to pay for his costs of living. In fact, for the Minister of Finance to suggest that somehow job creation will be the salvation of the pensions of senior citizens is absolutely absurd and ridiculous. In fact, it is an insult to seniors that he could stand in his place in Question Period today and say that the Government would not be cutting their pensions in August, September, October or November. Does the Minister of Finance really think that the senior citizens are so stupid as not to realize that the provisions of this Budget will be the New Year's gift of the Conservative Party to the people of Canada in 1986? The New Year's bonus will be a 3 per cent annual reduction in the pensions they would have received, if the Minister of Finance had not delivered this heinous document in the House.
I can understand why the Minister was somewhat riled today during Question Period. We have a tradition in this Parliament that as does the Budget so does the Minister. The Minister is on the run. In the first political act of this Government, we have seen the true colour of the Conservative Party and the true colour of the Minister of Finance. We saw it in the committee this morning when the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate moved an amendment which said to the Government: "If you want to cut the pensions of senior citizens by 3 per cent every year over the next five years, we will cut your budget".
What did the Government House Leader say, in a knee-jerk reaction which was so typical of the Government's approach to senior citizens? He said that if we cut their pensions, they would cut the pensions of the poor. He cannot look at any other solutions. Again the Minister of Finance asked us in the House today to introduce some creative solutions or some suggestions. We have introduced suggestion after suggestion after suggestion.

Today, the Hon. Member for Laval-des-Rapides (Mr. Gar-neau) proposed another solution which would be to have the capital gains tax exemption available to 4 per cent of the population, the wealthiest in Canada. The money saved could then be spent on the Old Age Security pensions.
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is unable to understand our proposals because he does not understand the poverty of elderly Canadians. He only understands Bay Street politics. He only wants to give his Bay Street friends jobs and benefits. He knows he can give a $500,000 capital gains tax exemption, Mr. Chairman. Capital gains with no strings attached, a present for the 4 per cent of the Canadian people who can take advantage of the exemption.
Mr. Chairman, most elderly Canadians have never been able to earn $400,000 or $500,000. If he does not believe us, perhaps he will believe the letters coming in from across Canada. I have been getting letters from Newfoundland and Britsh Columbia, from elderly Canadians across the country who are asking us . . . There are not many of us in the Opposition. There are 40 in the Liberal Party and 30 in the New Democratic Party. However, we are fighting for the elderly because your so-called Conservative Members are saying nothing.
At least the Hon. Member for Western Arctic (Mr. Nickerson) had the courage today to table a petition concerning the problems of people in the North. But where are the other voices? Where are the voices of the Conservatives, the Members from Quebec who have remained silent, who have not said a word to protect our Canadian elderly? Where are they? We have a Conservative majority that made any number of promises to Canadians, but now, when the neediest in our society are being attacked, who is going to protect them? We are, the Liberal Party is. The Liberal Party fought to make the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) face up to the fact that he broke his word, that he did not keep the promise he made in Sherbrooke, that he actually lied or failed to tell Canadians the truth.
Mr. Chairman-

Perhaps I cannot say it as well as a constituent from Newfoundland who wrote to me. This particular constituent expressed well the message which would best go out, not only to Members and Ministers on the government side of the House, but to all those back-benchers over there who have not yet had the courage to rise in the House and speak out on this issue.
The letter reads:
Dear Prime Minister:
I write on behalf of myself and the other 22 old age pensioners of my small community who depend on our wee pensions as our sole income. Though I am 73 years of age now and disabled because of Parkinson's disease, 40 years ago I was like Mila; a young wife and mother, busily engaged in the war effort and raising a young family at the same time. We never had to go to Government for any hand-out... but believed we would enjoy our lives particularly those of us in an extended period of widowhood; drawing our earned pensions from a very grateful country's bounty and without fear of our meagre incomes being gnawed down in buying power every year through inflation. Now, we are below the poverty line. We have all done our share. Senior citizens should not be expected to pay off the deficit which has grown about 10 per cent-
I am sorry the Minister of Finance is not here to hear the facts which he should be laying on the Canadian table.
The letter continues:
-during the short period your administration has been in power-
The writer was referring to the Conservative administration.
-while the fat oil industry-personified to us by the television cameras shooting the soap opera, Dallas-are let off the hook in the blind hope that these rich mandarins and petromerchants... buy up more real estate in Florida and throughout the sunbelt states .. . The history of mankind and even true Conservative philosophy. .. corroborates that man is greedy and that the oil company billionaires whenever possible, will be takers rather than givers-
June 18, 1985

Please reconsider your decision to make us pay the piper... in the so-called sunset days of our lives? We did our share when our bodies were strong, our minds acute, our pockets almost empty but our spirits and optimism high.
We simply cannot be collectively nor individually expected to pay again and again. It is simply not fair, and if your Mr. Wilson is not brought to heel by you, fired or ordered to amend this ghastly Budget to offer us reasonable indexing relief we can never believe your word again. We, senior citizens, can only meet together and talk about the wrong you are seen by us to be intended to do commencing next January. Many of us may not even be around to vote against you when the next national election is called, but some of us shall be and others will have "aged" into our non-chosen slots in society. Please do not add insult to injury by having your Ministers and your back-bencher apologists state that senior citizens who need their pensions to exist, will ever truly support this dastardly act? I think we can write enough letters in the coming months to offset that claim and to place such statements in the same trash can as "your campaign one relating to "sacred trusts" ".
I have discussed this letter amongst my peers and all degree I should send it to you having supported my stand wholeheartedly.
This particular letter was written by Bridget Laurie from St. Thomas, Newfoundland. I have received letters from across Canada. This is another letter from Newfoundland from another senior citizen who believed the Conservative Government when the Prime Minister said that pensions would not be touched.
The back-bencher who does not have the courage to get up and speak against this Budget asks whether my interventions are in order. They are in order because the amendment moved by the Member for Gander-Twillingate is telling the Government quite clearly that if it wants to penalize the senior citizens of the country by 3 per cent, it will have to cut its spending by 3 per cent. We are prepared to support a borrowing Bill to give the Government billions and billions of dollars at the same time as that self-same hypocritical Conservative Government is telling the senior citizens of the country that they will be cut, cut and cut.
Is this the New Year's present for which the senior citizens voted when last September they joined with Canadians from coast to coast to give the Conservative Government an overwhelming mandate? No, they were tricked and hoodwinked. They were fooled by a Government and a Prime Minister who, day after day, made promises which he never intended to keep. They were fooled by a Finance Minister who has now shown the Canadian people quite clearly that he is more interested in lining the pockets of his rich friends than he is in helping those in society who can least afford to pay.
I believe there are a number of Members on the government side of the House who do not support this measure. I believe that the caucus meeting of the Conservative Party last week was a heated one. Young people from coast to coast have shown their courage and said that they will pay the deficit, that they do not want their grandparents to bear the burden of that deficit. Mr. Chairman, I believe the Government wants to reverse its position. It realizes that the power of senior citizens across the country is not to be tampered with and that the support which put this Government in office came, in large measure, from the very senior citizens whom the Government is now seeking to destroy and cut back.
Borrowing Authority Act

Mr. Chairman, it is quite obvious that many Members-and not only in the Liberal Party-expect the Prime Minister to take action. Last night in Manicouagan they were expecting the Prime Minister to be true to his word, if that is possible. He even stated in his own book that if he were to make a mistake he would not be ashamed to change his mind. Judging from letters received from across the country, from Newfoundland, from British Columbia, from Ontario, from my own riding, from Hamilton with a petition bearing more than 1,000 signatures, and Friday there will be a gathering where 200, 300, 400, 500 elderly people will come from my constituency to tell this Government what they think of this measure against old age pensioners. We are waiting from some kind of response from the Prime Minister. Before the adjournment, Mr. Chairman, why can he not do something in the House this week by offering an anniversary present to all elderly Canadians who are impatiently waiting for an answer from the Government? There is political unrest throughout the country right now. Mr. Chairman, such unrest means that elderly people are speaking up in most cities to tell their Members, be they Conservatives, Liberals or New Democrats: We do not want our pensions reduced. We do not want to have to pay again and again. We cannot afford to pay more because we already live below the poverty line.

While the Minister of Finance is seeking borrowing authority for these billions of dollars and telling the people of Canada that they are supposed to cut back and that seniors of the country will have to bear the burden, what can he say to Mr. Gabriele in my riding? Mr. Guiseppe Gabriele has to support a family. There are some seniors who have children who are still at home. He has to support a wife and a child on a combined monthly income of $904.68. His combined expenses are $953.67. Therefore, he is a net loser every month of approximately $49. He has reached the point where he is even seeking help to be able to afford to pay the taxes on his home.
Can the Minister of Finance tell Mr. Gabriele where he is going to get the extra $30 a month that he will lose as a result of these punitive measures in the old age pension and the family allowance? The deindexation of the family allowance is another insidious tax on families which can least afford to pay. That is another example of the distorted priorities of a Government which will give oil companies $1 billion or $2 billion. It will give people who can afford to have capital gains $.5 million. Yet, with regard to the senior citizens and families of the country, the Government says, "Let them eat cake".
I urge all Members on the government side of the House who feel the same as I do to prevail upon the Minister of Finance to retract and to prevail upon the Prime Minister to keep his word. People believed him. Government Members have a responsibility to force the Prime Minister to uphold his promise to the Canadian people because, by forgoing that promise, he has shown the Canadian people what the Conservative Party and the Conservative Government are really all

about. It is a blue-blooded Party for the rich. We knew that before September 4, and now the Party is exposing itself in all its hideousness to the people of Canada.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I am pleased to take part in this debate on a motion which proposes a 3 per cent reduction in the borrowing authority sought by the Government. I would be overjoyed to be able to join in a debate on a motion for an increase in the amount of borrowing authority if it would ensure the capacity of the Government to cancel deindexation. However, since the rules of the House do not allow us to move in that direction, I shall take part in the present debate.
It is obvious that the actions of the Government have aroused the anger and outrage of many Canadians. That is certainly true in the City of Thunder Bay and in other parts of northwestern Ontario with which I am in touch. I find it astonishing that government Members do not have the same experience. I would like them to hear from some of my constituents regarding their feelings about the Government's actions. I received a copy of a letter which was addressed to the Minister of Finance and was sent by two senior citizens of my riding, Elsie and Wilfred Harrison. They write as follows:
My wife and I are recipients of O.A.S. Pensions, we are also in that category where we do not qualify to receive any portion of the G.I. Supplement, and to continue in this avenue may I say that as of the last return we made to "Internal Revenue" we did not qualify to pay any Income Tax. That, sir, will tell you what our financial level is.
During your Budget Speech, and on several occasions since, I have heard you say that if and when the indexing of O.A.S. Pensions is introduced-that is, when the increase will cover only the amount over 3 per cent-the recipient of the pension will not be hurt.
Sir, you have said it once too often for my liking, so I am writing this letter to tell you that if this miserly item is introduced in 1986, my wife and 1 will be poorer, and in subsequent years, we shall be yet poorer. We, my wife and I, together with our friends cannot understand in what circles you move where "many" people say that this item will not hurt them. Most emphatically will we be hurt, together with thousands of others.
Writing in a similar vein is another senior constituent of mine named Miss K. R. Escott, who writes as follows in a letter that was addressed to me personally:
I wish to add my name to the large number of voters who are unhappy with the 1985 budget as presented by Mr. Wilson and approved by Mr. Mulroney.
They definitely have taken from those who have not to benefit those who have.
I would suggest that both Mr. Wilson and Mr. Mulroney "tighten their belts" for the next five years to the degree where each of these men are compelled to live on the basic old age pension for the remainder of their elected term.
That suggestion would certainly drive the lesson home for Ministers of the Crown who think that this particular sacrifice can be borne with equanimity by our seniors.
Next I have a letter from another constituent, one who has the good fortune to be employed by the grain elevators of Thunder Bay. In another area, he experienced the cancellation of the home ownership savings plan to which he had been contributing for six years. He feels very strongly about that. In reference to the cancellation of the home ownership savings plan, he begins a paragraph by stating:
Also while I'm on the subject of cheating I would like to state that I do not like the way this Government has treated my Grandmother and the senior citizens of this country. You would think that in the 80's the government would stop picking on the people who made this country.
Is there no law against this dictatorship and to what depth will this new Government sink to? In the election the people have trusted the Conservative Party with the affairs of this country ... and it seems that the people will have to suffer because of the lies that we have been fed.
I hope that you, Ian Angus and Ed Broadbent, will keep reminding the Canadian people of the mistake that was made in 1984. Make sure that the people know that the Conservatives are for the rich. And that they don't forget it.
He concludes with the following observation:
-I feel that these fat cat Conservatives should be put on the budget and earnings of an "Ordinary Canadian" and then made to tighten their belts.
This letter was sent to me by Jim Fiorito, one of my constituents who is employed in the elevator industry. He was recently married and has a daughter. He is concerned about his grandmother and other seniors.
I have a fourth letter which was sent to me from another working man although he is closer to retirement age than the previous writer and has a wife who is already receiving a pension. Mr. Ewald Dombrowsky writes as follows:
-the Budget is very unfair not only for pensioners but also for ordinary Canadians. Where are the Jobs, Jobs, Jobs!!?? ... Our son is unemployed already 2x/i years, he has a family (3 boys) and nothing is coming up here. It is a hard situation.
We hope, you and the New Democratic Party will continue working to ensure fairness for all Canadians.
That last sentence, of course, relates very nicely to the question to which I referred in passing, which is, why is it that members of the Opposition receive letters of this sort and see constituents coming into their offices in large numbers signing petitions to protest the action of the Government while government Members claim not to be seeing that? They may of course be refusing to pass on that information.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare did not appreciate the suggestion that his riding office in southeastern Manitoba was putting constituents on hold when they called in to complain about the pensions, and I can well imagine that he did not appreciate that suggestion. I take it, though, that government Members are not encouraging their constituents in any way to protest the actions the Government has taken and are trying to enforce that regime of silence, which was surely the Government's hope when the Budget was brought down on May 23, a regime of silence in which people in the various quarters would swallow their medicine or run off with the gains that the Budget would give them, each mourning or rejoicing in solitude and silence that which the Budget did.
Surely if members of the Government were to seek the honest opinions of their constituents, there would not be much doubt about what those constituents think. I would suggest to people all across the country, and in fact to all those who are watching us this afternoon, enjoying what we are debating and hoping that it will have an effect on the Government, to make sure that the Prime Minister, who is ultimately responsible for these things, hears from them.
June 18, 1985

The Minister of Finance does what the Prime Minister tells him to do. Quite clearly, he was on about a six-inch leash yesterday while the Prime Minister mulled over how to get out of the terrible hole he has got himself into regarding this monumental political mistake. I would like to be sure that the Prime Minister at least is aware of what Canadians think, so 1 urge people all across the country to write to the Prime Minister at Room 309-S here in the House of Commons Ottawa, Ontario, K1A 0A2, and be very sure to get those letters in because the Prime Minister's Office certainly wants to know what Canadians think about the actions of Government, good and ill.
In this case, we have an ill action by the Government and constituents ought to let the Prime Minister know that they do not approve. They ought to urge him on this process of cogitation in which he is clearly involved these days as he determines how he can cancel this particular proposal of the Budget without at the same time cancelling the career of the Minister of Finance.
Canadians do want to keep putting on the pressure so that the Government keeps the promises it made during the election campaign of last summer and remains faithful to the expectations that were aroused in the minds of Canadians from coast to coast as more and more extravagant promises were made, even though the Conservative Leader and his Party were well aware of the financial position of the country and well aware of the need that existed for the Government to deal with all those challenges that will get us back toward the full employment that we all seek. I thank you, Mr. Chairman, for giving me the opportunity this afternoon to put some of my constituents' comments on the record and to urge Canadians to put the pressure on this Government that it deserves regarding this very unfortunate feature of the Budget.

speechtext:
From the outset of the debate on this amendment, Mr. Chairman, it is obvious that we want to establish clearly the intentions of the Official Opposition and the reason why we moved it. Quite simply, Mr. Chairman, ever since the Budget was tabled we find it unfair and inequitable. We on this side of the House, Mr. Chairman, have tried every means to make Government Members, more particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), understand that it is unacceptable in a modern society like ours in 1985 that the deficit be reduced by favouring the rich and attacking the poorest people in our society, Mr. Chairman. Those are poor people who have only their old age security pension, and more particularly others who get nothing more than the pension and the guaranteed income supplement. Mr. Chairman, all Canadians know very well that when we talk about the guaranteed income supplement we are referring to very old and very poor people.
I would invite the Prime Minister to visit my riding of Bourassa. I would also invite the Minister of Finance to visit my beautiful riding of Bourassa and face the elderly residents
Borrowing Authority Act
of Manoir Aimee-Leonard, face the elderly residents of Manoir Gouin, every one of them aged 65 or more, face the senior citizens of Angelica and Cascade homes for the aged, face the senior citizens of Tours Gouin, Sainte-Rita home for the aged, Manoir de Montreal, Manoir l'Escapade, Residence du Confort-it may be called Residence du Confort, but they are elderly people-Residence Manoir Tremblay, Montreal North, and the 15 Golden Age Clubs.
One thing for sure, Mr. Chairman, is that if the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance were to agree to meet with people in my riding and ask them whether they are prepared to accept the 3 per cent deindexation, they would be told: Mr. Prime Minister, what about your election promises, particularly your sacred promise to maintain full indexation? Mr. Prime Minister, you may rest assured that Canadians will remember, and let me tell you something I like to repeat often-you have fooled Canadians on September 4. As the saying goes in English:
"You can fool some of the people some of the time, but you can't fool all of the people all of the time, Mr. Prime Minister".

That bears repeating and as the saying goes, you can fool some Canadians some of the time, but you certainly cannot fool them all the time, Mr. Prime Minister. Once again to the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, through you, Mr. Chairman: Do you have enough heart, audacity and guts to meet with elderly people and tell them that deindextion will cost them $1,500 within five years? Do you have that kind of courage, Mr. Prime Minister? And now to Conservative Members, Members on the Government side, this is a humane not a partisan issue, we are not trying to defeat the Government and, as I said, we are not trying to score political points. We are simply asking for very humanitarian treatment. All we are asking is that you urge the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance to reconsider their decision, urge them not to go ahead with deindexation of old age security pensions, and not think it over month after month and thus keep elderly people in a state of anxiety for six, seven or eight months. And 1 would ask the Hon. Members opposite to ensure this is done as soon as possible.
Mr. Chairman, thousands and thousands of people from coast to coast in this country are protesting against the unfairness and inadequacy of this measure. The Quebec National Assembly has also passed a unanimous resolution condemning the measure and urging the Government of Canada to reverse a decision it considers to be a demonstration of flagrant injustice towards senior citizens who are among the neediest in our society.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I have been here for some 17 or 18 Budgets speeches, Budget Bills and borrowing authority Bills, and this is the first time I can recall that neither the Minister of Finance, nor the Minister of State for Finance or their Parliamentary Secretaries are in the House.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Order!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
1 have never seen it happen before. When the Government of Canada is borrowing $18 billion, one would think that this would have some kind of high priority. I hope we are not being left to the tender mercies of the Secretary of State for External Affairs, but I see he is sitting in front of the officials from the Department of Finance. If we are being left to his tender mercies, then we are doomed again.
There is a myth being circulated in this country, Mr. Chairman, about the amounts which Governments borrow and their fantastic deficits. In fact, this Government and its predecessors, both Liberal and Tory, have been hypnotized by the deficit. I would hope that there is an Hon. Member in the Cabinet who can answer some questions about the deficit.
Deficits are accrued because we borrow money to pay off previous borrowings and to pay current bills. We also borrow money to invest in the future of the country. What I do not understand as an innocent prairie boy, Mr. Chairman, is that the deficit in 1945 was much higher than it is now and if you put it in 1985 dollars, the deficit at the end of the Second World War was about two or three times as high as it is now. 1 recall, as an innocent prairie boy, hearing the experts, the financial columnists, the Tories and the Grits all screaming about the deficit. I would like to direct some questions if, as and when the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance or one of their Parliamentary Secretaries arrive.
In the first place, if we put this money for which borrowing authority is sought into housing, into cleaning up our air and water, into reforestation and a whole host of other projects, that would not be a deficit expenditure. It would be an investment.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: We are doing that.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That would reduce unemployment. Is there anyone around on the government side who can tell me, Mr. Chairman, if it is not correct that if we reduce unemployment now from the 11 per cent to the 12 per cent range down to 7 per cent or 7.5 per cent, we will wipe out the deficit within three years?
There is another area I would like to touch on, and 1 hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will pay attention.
June 18, 1985

Last year the federal Government paid $21 billion in interest on the national debt. Of course, the financial experts emphasized the enormity of that amount. It was at least 5 per cent of the Gross National Product. It required one-third of the Government's revenue, which amounted to $2,500 per taxpayer, to pay the interest on the national debt. That is in 1984. There is a notable oversight there. Ninety per cent of that $21 billion in interest was paid to Canadians. That is the proportion of the federal government bonds held in Canada. The average Canadian taxpayer, if you averaged out the $21 billion, received almost $2,500 in interest. So that all that happened was that we were lending money out and paying ourselves back. In fact, the Government received almost the same amount back as it paid out in interest charges on this mythical deficit.
There is another angle, Mr. Chairman, and I hope the Secretary of State for External Affairs will think about this as well. The Bank of Canada, our central bank, responsible for regulating the national money supply, held government bonds in 1984 to the tune of $17 billion. That is about 10 per cent of the total outstanding debt. The Bank of Canada is wholly owned by the federal Government and the people of Canada. At the end of each calendar year it turns over its net revenue to the Government of Canada. So in 1984, the Bank of Canada received $1,981 billion in interest on the federal bonds it held. It had an operating cost of $129 million. Therefore, the Bank of Canada returned to the Government of Canada $1,832,000,000. Thus the Government of Canada received back 93 per cent of the money it paid as bond interest to the Bank of Canada in 1984. So what is the reason for all this terror and hypnotism on the government side about the deficit?
In 1939, the federal Government paid out only $135 million on a $21 billion debt compared to the $21 billion it paid out in 1984. That is nearly 200 times more last year than in 1939. But the average Canadian lived pretty poorly in 1939. The unemployment level across the country was at 15 per cent. People were on welfare and some joined the Army in order to receive a dollar a day. If what applied then were to apply now, according to the financial exports and the Minister of Finance when he talks about his deficit, I suppose Canadians would be running around eating scraps and wearing rags. The whole mythology of the deficit is not how much the deficit is, but what the deficit is for. The fact is that in all its domestic borrowings, the Government takes back almost as much as it borrows. What it pays out in interest charges it takes back in taxes. That has always been the case and there is nothing new about it.
This might sound like sacrilege around here, but why not add about three billion bucks to this borrowing authority to be put into housing, reforestation and cleaning up our air and water? It will put people to work earning income, paying taxes, and reducing the deficit.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
And increase inflation.
Borrowing Authority Act

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: It has been done a number of times before by various and sundry Liberal and Tory Governments. They did not buy the Proposition 13 syndrome imported from California. How much of this borrowing is going to go into job creation and reducing the deficit? Not a nickel. It is all going to go off into the same vicious circle. You borrow the money from the taxpayers and collect it back in almost equal amounts. That is where the mythology is in this nonsense about deficits. One thing my friends opposite forget is that you cannot compare an individual living above his means and borrowing beyond his capacity to repay his debt with a Government which has done the same thing because the essential difference is that governments can tax people from whom they borrow the money.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That is what you want to do.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That is exactly what you are doing. You tax them to pay for the money you borrowed from them. No little storekeeper, farmer or fisherman can do that. If he runs a deficit, he has to rake it up all by himself. But Governments are different, municipal, provincial and federal. They tax the people they borrow money from and that is how they pay off the borrowings. If I, an innocent prairie boy, am wrong, I hope someone will get up and correct me. I would like to know from someone over there or from the Department of Finance whether it was correct that 90 per cent of the $21 billion in interest payments last year on our debt was paid to Canadians, and that the average Canadian bond holder got about $2,500 from the Government. In turn, the Government taxed them for slightly over $2,400 on those interest earnings. If I am not correct, I hope someone will get up and tell me so and show me so.
We all appreciate the fact that the Government needs to have revenue, and much has been said by some of my colleagues about the options available to a Government of any party, and I want to return to a matter 1 have raised in every budget debate since 1968. At that time, deferred corporate taxes amounted to a little under $20 billion. They now amount to around $35 billion. No other citizen, individual farmer, fisherman, small storekeeper or anyone else, can defer his taxes. Just try it and you will have Revenue Canada on your neck. But there is in excess of $35 billion in deferred corporate taxes on the books of this country, and if the Government would care to charge the bank rate or 1 per cent over prime as interest on those deferred corporate taxes, you would have about $3.5 billion to put people to work and reduce the deficit. In fact, you would be surprised at how many corporations would be rushing forward to reduce their deferred corporate taxes. You would be amazed, because they would not want to face that interest bill every year. How about that? That is not some socialist dogma. If you lend someone money, you charge him interest, pure and simple. So let us give him a reasonable break; 9 per cent interest on the deferred corporate taxes.
Mr. Chairman, the tragedy is that every year we go through a borrowing authority exercise and we get the free enterprise Governments hypnotized by the size of the deficit, but they do

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
not tell us the whole story. They never have. They do not tell us that most of the borrowings are held by Canadians and it is Canadians who collect the interest. It is Canadians who pay back most of the interest in income taxes. They would pay back more if we had a fair tax system. Well, I would be inclined, if the Government were to come in with an amendment to the borrowing authority Bill, to put $1 billion into housing. Every city in this country has a waiting list as long as your arm for chronic care beds and rooms in senior citizens' homes. I would put $1 billion into cleaning up our air and water. You could put 200,000 young people to work there. Then another $1 billion should go into transportation and reforestation or whatever else. We did it during the war, and we ran a deficit that in 1985 dollars is three times a high as the one we have now. We only had a population of 10 million people then. So do not give me that nonsense about reducing the deficit at the expense of old age pensioners, farmers, fishermen and little storekeepers. It sure as heck is not going to bother Imperial Oil, not at all, not a nickel's worth. Who are we representing here? Make up your minds.
I think it is a travesty, Mr. Chairman, when we are talking about the financing of this country, that we do not have in attendance the Minister of Finance or the Minister of State for Finance. Neither are their Parliamentary Secretaries here.
