subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
As you know, Bill C-51 would give borrowing authority to the Canadian Government and if it is adopted the Minister of Finance and the Progressive Conservative Government would be authorized to borrow $18.2 billion between now and the end of the current fiscal year. It is therefore an extremely important measure within a rather special context, namely the debate over deindexation of old age security pensions.
Mr. Chairman, I consider the debate quite inappropriate in the present context, when we read newspapers and particularly when we hear the Prime Minister answer questions put to him. For instance, I refer to The Globe and Mail of today, June 18, where I can read under the byline of Mr. Richard Cleroux a report from Sept-Iles whose first paragraph is rather significant:

"Prime Minister Brian Mulroney said last night that the part in Finance Minister Michael Wilson's Budget dealing with pensions for the elderly "deserves to be reviewed" ".
June 18, 1985



And further on, still in quotation marks, the article reports the Prime Minister as saying this:

"Mr. Mulroney described the section of the Budget that eliminates part of the protection against inflation for pensioners as troubling".

So said the Prime Minister of the country, Mr. Chairman, and his Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has just tabled a Budget in which he proposes partial deindexation of old age security pensions beginning January 1, 1986. All Members who sit in this House must be rather embarrassed to read remarks such as those quoted in today's Globe and Mail.
Where the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) indicated that the Budget of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) "deserves to be reviewed", and further on, where he used the word "troubling" in referring to the section of the Budget dealing with partial deindexation of Old Age Security pensions, Mr. Chairman, we are entitled to ask ourselves today whether this is not just a big public relations scenario to prepare the public for a political about-face. And if that is the case, I wish the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier) would advise this House immediately so that we can stop talking about a question that could be settled without debate. But if that is not the Government's intention, and there is no indication from the Government benches that what the Prime Minister said yesterday in Sept-Iles is to be taken seriously, we will have to continue this debate, because there is no other way for the Official Opposition to bring to the attention of the Government benches and public opinion the fact that we are in total disagreement with this political decision. Mr. Chairman, a Budget is an expression of certain choices. When a Minister of Finance starts preparing his Budget, he has a series of options. And this afternoon when I heard the Minister of Finance informing the House, with dramatic emphasis, that he could not say right away whether the Government was going to maintain full indexation because the financial situation was so terrible, because they had to reduce the deficit, because of the terrible legacy they were left by the Liberals-
Mr. Chairman, the Minister of Finance had a choice. He had options. He had the option of maintaining full indexation of Old Age Security pensions, and in 1985-86, according to the figures we were given, that would cost him $15 million more, which is not particularly earthshaking as the Parliamentary Secretary would agree, and in 1986-87 it would cost $250 million.
Mr. Chairman, so everyone will understand that the Minister of Finance had an alternative, and his officials here facing his Parliamentary Secretary know as well as I do that he had an
Borrowing Authority Act
option: the option of deciding where he was going to put his money. Take the capital gains tax exemption, for instance. This was an option the Minister of Finance had, and he decided to forego $300 million in tax revenue in 1985-86, by granting this exemption to the wealthy in our society.
If we take the $300 million and add to that another option the Minister had ad which he exercised, namely, to forego $240 million in 1985-86 by removing the Oil Export Charge, and if we add that amount to the previous amount, we get a total of $540 million.
It seems Old Age Security pensions cost the Government $8.5 billion, and 3 per cent of $8.5 billion for one-third of the year adds up to approximately the same figure. So the Minister of Finance-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: That is where the money went!

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
The Minister of Finance had an option, and 1 remember what the Prime Minister said in that televised debate: "Sir, you had an option." That is what the present Prime Minister told the former Prime Minister. I say to the Prime Minister today: "Sir, you had an option, and you decided to give the money to the rich and take it away from some of the elderly of this country."
You had an option and you exercised that option. And do not tell the House today that by exercising that option, by giving more money in the form of tax exemptions to the oil multinationals, and tax exemptions on capital gains, do not tell the House that now that you have exercised that option, you have no money left for the elderly. There can be no double standard, and I say to the Minister of Finance: "Sir, you had an option. You had an option." Basically, Mr. Chairman, when we analyze the issue of deindexing pensions for senior citizens, we find that it is all a matter of budgetary options. What I want to do in the next few minutes is to analyse the economic philosophy and general orientation of the Budget.
I should immediately point out that, when I look at this Bill asking for a borrowing authority of $18 billion, which is directly related to the budgetary options, I am not concerned only with the deindexing, or partial deindexing of old age security pensions and family allowances. I disagree with the basic philosophy behind this Bill, with the choices made by this Government and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). The figures which I made public and which have yet to be questioned show that, contrary to what the Prime Minister said before the Budget was brought down and contrary to what the Minister of Finance said during his speech, the Budget is not fair and equitable to the taxpayers. For my part, I would say, and I shall try to prove it, that this Budget is unfair and inequitable to the middle income group in our society which is the group most affected. In addition, the borrowings author-

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
ized by this Bill will affect this group by giving them a heavier tax burden.
In accordance with its philosophy, the Government talks a lot about the private sector. The Government wants the private sector to invest and to create jobs, and at the same time, by massive tax increases, it reduces the purchasing power of those who make up the market for Canadian businesses. These massive tax increases made Mr. Reynold of the Wall Street Journal say that the Government wanted to tax the economy to prosperity.

The Government wants to tax the economy to prosperity.
[ Translation]
Mr. Chairman, I have prepared a few government budgets in my life time, I have read some others, I have had an opportunity as severale other Members in this House to monitor the economic situation in Canada and other provinces, but it is the first time I see any government maintain it has made the right choice when deciding to promote economic growth by way of massive tax increases. This is the first time this would be done.
Those additional taxes which the Government does not like to be told about, that shower of taxes, will take $12 billion worth of purchasing power away from middle-income Canadians in 1990-91 alone. By the end of this decade, with those tax increases imposed on middle-income groups, not to mention other sectors, but looking only at middle-income groups, those tax increases combined with the de-indexing of old age pensions and family allowances will result in the most significant part of our society which represents the market box, our businesses, being rabbed of $37 billion in purchasing power. In terms of dollars, this is twice as much as the Bill now before us.
The general thrust of the budget, the general thrust of the policy behind the budget is basically wrong is my view. Deindexing old age pensions is not the only thing that is unfair and unjust-the whole budget thrust is slashing so many billions of dollars, $37 billion in purchasing power from middle-income groups and senior citizens, this Government is reducing the ability of those consumers to buy goods and services from Canadian businesses.
On the one hand, the Government is reducing purchasing power, our businesses' market, and on the other hand it is asking those same businesses to create jobs. Moreover, the Government has taken a most dangerous road by putting all its eggs in two main baskets, the first being energy, especially oil energy, and the second being Canadian exports to the United States. From the first basket, oil corporations will be getting a tax break that will total $8.5 billion by the end of the decade.
And I say to the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Lanthier): This is a clear-cut and specific example of a choice. The Minister of Finance had a choice, he had two or three options. He chose to give money to the oil
multinationals. Thereafter he should not be telling us he has no more money for senior citizens because the deficit must be reduced. He should tell us candidly, honestly that they had a choice to make and they chose one area rather than the other. So he had a choice, and his option means $8.5 billion in tax benefits to oil multinationals. Even considering that eventually certain grants will not be allowed, that is a net cost of between $4.5 and $5 billion in revenue lost to the multinationals by the end of the decade. They are hoping that those multinational corporations will invest, and that this will create jobs in Canada. So much for the first level, the second being exports.
Because the purchasing power of the Canadian people is being considerably eroded, we have to rely on our exports as a means to support our economy. If I am coming back to the subject of the oil companies, it is because their decision whether or not to invest will be determined by the extent of the market as well as the prices. Those, as it is well known, are dictated by OPEC, the Organization of Oil Exporting Countries. As to the market, it will be influenced by the value of the Canadian dollar and the over all growth of the Canadian economy. Well, these variables are quite uncertain, and insisting on putting all our eggs in the same basket would prove very risky indeed for the future of our economy and especially for our young people who are looking for jobs.
Mr. Chairman, recently I read in Business Week an analysis which had been prepared as the result of consultations with many experts and which indicated that the price of oil could go down as low as $20 a barrel. Norway has already lowered its price to $26 a barrel, and OPEC has decided to hold its July meeting in June to deal with this emergency situation and to take remedial action in an effort to prevent an excessive drop in price. When I see the Government of Canada investing so much money in one single industry and being forced to burden Canadian taxpayers with such a heavy tax load to pay for the tax breaks given to multinational companies, I very seriously question the crucial choice it has made in this area, because I am not sure at all that it will yield the dividends so often mentioned by hon. members on the Government side.
In another basket are our exports: 75 per cent of our exports are directed towards the United States. Already, Mr. Chairman, the American Congress takes a critical view at foreign exports. Figures for the first three or four months indicate a trade deficit of $11.5 billion. For April, and since the beginning of the year, the trade deficit has reached $45 billion.
Mr. Chairman, when we consider a number of products, we realie how unsound was the choice made by the Minister of Finance. As far as steel, timber, hogs, beef and sugar are concerned-we will certainly have a potato war later on this year-we can expect that as long as the value of the U.S. dollar remain high, very strong lobbies in the Congress will pressure the American administration into imposing quotas. That is why I say that pushing our exports so overwhelmingly is quite a risky proposition and I submit that making this choice so
June 18, 1985

aggressively that the government had to cut the Canadian people's purchasing power is a huge mistake in terms of economic direction.
You are aware that members on the Government side love to blame the Liberals for the deficit. However, the turning point of this deficit was the 1981-82 crisis, and it occurred not only in Canada, but also in the United States and in most Western countries. When 1 have discussions with Tory members not only on party matters but also on economic policy, I often ask them: What would you have done at the time to deal with the crisis? Would you have reduced unemployment insurance payments to avoid increasing the deficit? Would you have refused to implement job creation programs during the winter and to provide employment for students? Would you have been content to sit still while people lost their jobs without giving them any assistance? I think that to ask this question is also to answer it. I note that, with a real growth of 4.7 per cent in the Gross National Product, the Conservative Government has maintained the Winter Works program as well as the summer employment program for students. We are witnessing a growth in the Gross National Product. What would you have done during the depression? Would you have said: We have nothing to give; we have to reduce the deficit. I believe that this is unrealistic and this is the cause of our present problem.
As a matter of fact, with a Gross National Product of between $350 billion and $400 billion, 1 do not think that the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) found a deficit of $7 billion or $8 billion completely unreasonable or disastrous. If that is what he thinks today, Mr. Chairman, if the President of the Treasury Board finds a deficit of $11 billion disastrous, I would like to ask him how come, after being in power since September 4 and saying all those things about it, his Government has come out with a Budget of $105 billion, which represents a larger increase than the increase in the consumer price index. This is all he could do for a Party which has based its whole political ideology on reducing the deficit. They do not even have the courage the limit the increase in expenditures to the increase in the cost of living.
Mr. Chairman, I can see that the time allotted to me has nearly expired, but I understand that our rules will allow me to come back to this matter later on and I shall continue my comments for the information of the President of the Treasury Board.

Mr. Chairman, I am also very pleased to take part in this debate. With your permission, I would like to tell this House that before getting into politics, I had the honour of serving as president of a community centre for about 10 years. Thanks to this experience, I have been able to learn about some of the concerns of our senior citizens and to understand them. I think that we would be burying our heads in the sand if we failed to recognize that most of our senior citizens, who are now retired, are from very large families or have many children themselves. Contrary to the present generation and young people today, they have unfortunately not enjoyed the same benefits from society as we have throughout the years. They are people who, in many cases, earned $10, $12, $15 a week and who, with such miserable and dreadful salaries, did not have the same opportunities as our young people today who are covered by all kinds of insurance. Fathers and mothers who then had the bad luck to have sick children, and as I said, families were much larger in those days, had to assume those responsibilities, pay those bills, and were often in debt for ten years or more because of the illness of a couple of children.

They are also people who have experienced something that, of course, we did not know, that is the 1929 depression. Those people have also gone through two major conflicts and have suffered numerous hardships and problems during their lifetime. I think that today, in 1985, those people have reached retirement age and God knows that it is a well-deserved retirement. If anyone ever deserved a happy retirement, it is our senior citizens of 65 and over. They are the ones who, after facing so many hardships and problems, have become apprehensive and suffer from some kind of trauma, and unfortunately those people are more often than not traumatized if their medicine is changed by a simple letter. In a word, they are easily traumatized. They have to plan and prepare their budget months in advance in order to buy not treats but the necessities of life. They realize that the economic situation in our country is difficult and painful. They understand that. But they are not ready to accept sole responsibility. Those people do not agree with the kind of policy often stated since the beginning of this debate, a policy stated by the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) when she said last week: "Our senior citizens can make a sacrifice! After all, they are only asked to give up as little as $1 per day. speechtext:
For the Hon. Member's information, I suggest he read Hansard where the Hon. Member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mrs. Bertrand) states, after talking to senior citizens, that most, if not all, had told her they were quite willing to give up what she estimated would be a dollar a day. I am sorry but that is not the right way to look at this problem, because a dollar a day means a lot more to a person who has to live on what he or she gets from the State than it does to someone who is still on the labour market.
Last week, Mr. Chairman, my colleagues, that is, the Hon. Member for Montreal-Sainte-Marie (Mr. Malepart) and the Hon. Member for Shefford (Mr. Lapierre), and I had the privilege of attending a meeting organized on the spur of the moment, where senior citizens were asked to come and express
their views and their reactions to what the Conservative Government was proposing to do. People came to see us from all over, from the ridings of Megantic-Compton-Stanstead, Brome-Missisquoi, Sherbrooke, from my own riding and from Shefford. In some cases, these people travelled 75 or 80 miles to come give us their comments, which they did quite spontaneously. In the circumstances, and I am sorry to have to say so, it is very significant, since the elderly are usually quite passive and more inclined to accept a situation. It really takes something very serious to make them react, and in this case over 200 people came to see us to talk about all sorts of things such as: The younger generation today can thank us for all the advantages and prosperity they have and they should remember that we helped to build the Canada they have today.
There were people who told us: Well, this is the month of June and I have already started to save enough to buy myself a dress for Christmas. Some senior citizens told us they had been saving for two months to buy themselves a radio. Others were saving to be able to pay for cablevision. Well, there was a whole series of statements like that in which people made the point that they had to save for months to pay for what we consider to be the basics of our daily lives. They have to save for months to pay for things that to me are absolutely essential, things we take for granted.
Senior citizens told us they would be very hard-pressed to meet the increasing number of obligations society imposes on them.
In spite of all that, Mr. Chairman, the elderly realize the Government has a deficit, that it has commitments and that it wants to create jobs. They realize all that. What they do not understand, however, and I think they have a perfect right not to understand, is when they are asked to make a small sacrifice after the Government decides to change the military's uniforms and increase our arm contingents in Europe, the oil companies get huge exemptions, and the capital gains tax is removed. Well, Mr. Chairman, you will agree that it does not take a Ph.D. or a seasoned politician to understand that there is a double standard here and that the injustice is absolutely flagrant. And the elderly are certainly not prepared to make a sacrifice and tighten their belts in that case, as the Government would have them do.
There is another aspect I think is important and which I think demonstrates the utter meanness of this proposal. Just imagine, someone who is let us say 75 years old and who is told: Listen, tighten your belt, in a few years everything will be o.k. and you will get full indexation. Just imagine, this person is 75. In a few years, that person may no longer be alive, after spending the last two or three or four years of his or her life in a terrible state of mind, paralyzed at the thought of not being able to pay for his or her very basic needs, not luxuries but
June 18, 1985

basics to which they are certainly entitled because these people certainly have deserved to have a decent life.
In concluding, I may say that the riding I have represented since 1979 has been plagued by many, many problems.
I represent the riding where the major city is Asbestos and no one can talk about Asbestos without thinking about a significant slowdown in mining, particularly asbestos mining. There was a time when the company had 3,000 people on the payroll, but barely 800 are still there now.
I also represent the riding which has been and still is the victim of problems inherent in today's footwear markets. I also represent the riding where many pork producers live. I also represent the riding which experienced a rather serious problem not so very long ago, as Members may recall, the possible shutdown of Domtar operations. As you may have noted there are quite a few problems in my riding but, over the past six years, notwithstanding all those problems, obstacles and economic woes, I have to say that never did a single issue raise such interest in my riding. Never did such a problem prompt so many people to come to my office and tell me: It is unacceptable, it does not make sense, do something about the terrible measure the Government wants to take.
All those problems no matter how crucial never generated as much energy and efforts as people are showing and making in connection with the old age security pensions deindexation.
In conclusion, it seems to me that if we were to stop and consider the issue for a moment, as my colleagues so eloquently suggested, we could identify, image or invent a mechanism which would enable the Government to look elsewhere for the money it wants to take away from the elderly, to get the money from wealthy and well-to-do people so as to protect senior citizens and give them the security they so richly deserve, senior citizens who are entitled to get what appears to me under the circumstances to be the vital minimum, something which is basic and quite essential.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak briefly to this amendment to the borrowing Bill that was moved this morning. We are now discussing the Government's budgetary measures and its ability to administer the funds that it is asking the House to give it.
The people of Glengarry-Prescott-Russell are not at all satisfied with the way the Government is managing the funds given to Parliament. The western region of the riding that I represent lies near the National Capital of our country and, therefore, a large number of federal public servants live there. During the last election campaign, many promises were made by government Members. In this document to which I have referred on several occasions, I have outlined 338 promises which had been made to the people of Canada and many of them to the people of the National Capital area, the people who work for the Government.
Borrowing Authority Act
We saw in the recent Budget cut-backs in federal employment. I do not seem to recall during the last election campaign hearing Conservative Members stating, "Vote for us and you will be fired". I do not recall the Hon. Member for Ottawa-Carleton, the Hon. Member for Ottawa West and other Hon. Members who represent the National Capital Region ever having stood up to the Minister of Finance, the Minister of State for Finance or the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State for Finance to say that that is not right and that the people of the ridings that they represent did not vote for those measures. They voted for a specific group of promises which were made. However, the Government is not delivering. Why is it that Conservative Members who have ridings in the National Capital Region are not speaking on behalf of the people who voted for them in the last election?
As we move farther away toward the eastern end of the National Capital Region, in the constituency which 1 represent, the standard of living decreases considerably. There is higher unemployment, which is not uncommon in other constituencies, and the people have very little money to spare. Those people have to live with a Government which has increased the price of gasoline and decreased the purchasing power of senior citizens' pensions. At the same time, the Government is squandering money on all kinds of other things, for itself, its friends and its relatives.
There is a capital gains exemption which a parliamentary committee had requested for the farmers of the country. The Government has now extended that exemption to people who own yachts and condominiums in Florida. Why is it that the Government has enough money to give a break to the people who own a condominium in Florida, when it has no money to assist the senior citizens?
The priorities of the Government are wrong. The people of my riding do not agree with the measures which this Government has taken. I am sure the majority of people in every riding of the country feel the same way. If Conservative Members were not muzzled, they would want to speak on this issue. That is okay. Those Members cannot stand and speak on the issue, so opposition Members will have to repeat it more often. We will do it on their behalf. Perhaps we could call them proxy speeches.
The Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition stated on Budget night:
It is a Budget of broken promises. It breaks the trust Mr. Mulroney said he was going to have with the Canadian people. It hits the average Canadian very hard.
It doesn't come right out and hit him, it does it in a sneaky and gutless way. The Budget lacks courage.
A Budget is not just a bunch of numbers. A Budget has to do with people and jobs, with human careers and with meaningful life.
When I look at the priorities of the Government, I can easily understand why Disraeli once said that a Tory Government was organized hypocrisy. The Government made many promises to the people of the country and it has failed to deliver on those promises.

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
I would like to quote the first promise which was made to senior citizens by the Conservative Party during the last election campaign. It reads:
Reinstate complete indexing of Old Age Pensions to the actual cost of living, as of January 1st, 1985.
That was a specific promise which was made by the Leader of the Conservative Party of Canada last August. The Prime Minister is now breaking that solemn promise. He is breaking that promise along with hundreds of other promises. The Government has no money for senior citizens, yet it has money to squander on other measures.
The debate today is about fairness. That is the issue about which we are talking. The Government wants to reduce the pensions of our seniors by 3 per cent. Opposition Members are saying that if that is the case, the Government can cut its expenditures by 3 per cent. We know that the people of Canada who are receiving Old Age Security in the amount of $276.34 a month cannot afford to give up any part of that cheque.
The Government is telling us that it will create jobs. As interesting as that may be, what is the policy? Is it a policy which tells our senior citizens to go out and work? If not, why are we asking senior citizens to contribute toward job creation? Most grandparents whom I know are beyond age 65 or age 70. They are not looking for jobs. Most of them are unable to work. As a society, we accepted long ago that those people should receive their pension and that the pension should be universal. That universality should not be destroyed at the rate of 3 per cent a year by the Conservative Government.
Why does the Government want the money? Yesterday I spoke about some of the squandering which is going on, the abuses and the appointments of relatives and friends. Today we discovered, through the media, that the secretary of State for External Affairs has published a book. The book is entitled: The Right Honourable Brian Mulroney, Canada's eighteenth Prime Minister. It is rather unusual that the book was printed by the Secretary of State for External Affairs, for reasons which we all know. The book has many pictures of the Prime Minister. I am sure that hundreds of thousands of dollars were spent on it. In order to restore every senior citizen's pension in my riding, it would cost only $60,000 for one year. The Government should scrap the book, take the funds and give back the pensions to the senior citizens. I would like to quote from the book. It reads:
The work of raising living standards, creating opportunity and recognizing the equality of human beings is one to which we are committed-
The Prime Minister said that. What happened to the Prime Minister who was committed to equality? This book was written very recently. The ink is probably still wet. The same Prime Minister and his Minister of Finance, who were committed to equality and improving the standards of human beings, are now reducing the pensions of seniors. On page 2 of the book there is a lovely picture of the Prime Minister in his office. On the third page, the Prime Minister is quoted as saying:
There is no obligation more compelling, no duty more irresistible in Canada and around the world than to ensure that our minorities, linguistic and otherwise, live at all times in conditions of fairness and justice.
Of course, we know that that was seconded by the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Assiniboine, the whole view about linguistic minorities and otherwise.
This document talks about equality. It talks about protecting people. However, this Government acts in a completely opposite way. There are pages and pages in this document about money which was spent by the taxpayers of Canada to pay for the extravagance of this Government. The Government says we should give it some money. My constituents think otherwise, Mr. Chairman.
I tabled in this House yesterday a petition signed by many people from my riding. I have another petition here which I will be introducing in the House tomorrow. This petition was signed by the senior citizens of L'Orignal, Ontario. These people, like many other people across this country, object to the cut in the purchasing power of their Old Age Security cheque which the Minister of Finance and the Prime Minister want to perpetrate on them. The Minister of National Health and Welfare has said in this House that no one wants to cut anything.
What the Minister of National Health and Welfare is doing in this House and elsewhere is trying to convince the people that the Government is not cutting their cheque. He is saying that the cheque will not be less, it is just going to be increased less. In other words, if the cost of living increases by 5 per cent, the pension cheque will be increased by 2 per cent.
I see the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance sitting across from me and I know that he will want to set the record straight, so let me do it for him, Mr. Chairman. I am sure he will agree with me, being an economist, that if inflation increases by 5 per cent and the pension cheque is only increased by 2 per cent, no matter how you cut it, the purchasing power of that cheque is decreased. There is no other way of looking at it. For the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance to try to somehow get the senior citizens to believe that this is not so is not being perfectly honest. They know that our senior citizens know better. They know that if the cost of living increases by 5 per cent and their cheque is increased by 2 per cent, then a step backward of 3 per cent has been taken. That is easy for senior citizens to understand and just maybe this Government should give our senior citizens a little bit more credit. They have been around far longer than myself, the Minister and his Parliamentary Secretary.
Of course, our senior citizens are quite aware of what is going on and that is why they are protesting this measure so vehemently. The Minister of Finance and others are saying that the Opposition Parties are prompting the senior citizens of this country to rebel agains this budgetary measure. I ask you again, Mr. Chairman, is the Government giving the credit due to our senior citizens when it thinks that anyone can stand anywhere and say anything and that the senior citizens will
June 18, 1985

believe it? Is that all the credit and respect the Government has for the seniors of this country? It seems so, Mr. Chairman.
This Government refuses to believe that if the senior citizens are asking for something, it is a legitimate request. The Government refuses to believe it. It thinks it is the fault of the Opposition, but it is not the Opposition who wrote that Budget. It was the Conservative Government and those Hon. Members opposite who right now are hiding their heads in shame over this Budget. I don't blame the Members of the Government I see seated in the back rows on the Government side, almost with tears in their eyes over this Budget. If I were a Tory right now, I would be embarrassed as well. Heaven forbid that would ever happen, Mr. Chairman, and I am sure it won't. It is said that happiness is never having to say you're Tory, and I intend to remain happy.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I suggest all those speeches are very interesting, but I feel sad when I listen to them. What is basic to all those speeches is the will to stop the Government for a few moments, perhaps a few hours, while trying at the same time to make Government Members realize the seriousness of what they are doing about de-indexation.
This Government's intention to limit the indexing of Old Age Security pensions is irresponsible for all practical purposes. Admittedly, Mr. Chairman, a new government, an inexperienced government can make mistakes. But that kind of mistake is unforgivable. So much so that senior citizens across
Borrowing Authority Act
the land are launching campaigns against a Government that should be defending them, in order to have it back down.
In my own Province of New Brunswick, the movement is gathering speed. The New Brunswick Federation of Senior Citizens last week sent a very clear message to the Progressive Conservative Government. In a press release issued on behalf of its 30,000 members, the Chairperson of the Federation, Mrs. Edna Bourque, stated that recent changes announced by the Federal Minister of Finance are seriously disturbing the peaceful life and severely affecting the quality of life of senior citizens.
Mr. Chairman, the New Brunswick Federation of Senior Citizens is a very important association. As I said, it has a membership of 30,000, and speaks for 265 senior citizens' clubs who have joined the Federation to date. In other words, this Federation is representative of all senior citizens in the Province of New Brunswick.
There is no doubt that the members of the Federation feel that this Government's proposal is cruel, insensitive, and even immoral as it was said. If this Government would listen or had listened to what senior citizens in Canada had to say, certainly it would be ashamed of ever having proposed to de-index old age pensions. Senior citizens have come to me, saying the Government had no right to ask senior citizens to make sacrifices. I was told: "Who do they think they are to decide that senior citizens must make sacrifices?" Mr. Chairman, history tells us that the people being asked once again to make sacrifices are the very same people who have lived through the Great Depression of the late 20's and early 30's. They have also been through World War II. When I think of all the sacrifices which those people have had to make, I do not feel we should or can force them to live through more years of poverty, because a very large number of our senior citizens already live below the poverty line. In New Brunswick, to be more specific, more than 73 per cent of our senior citizens live below the poverty line. How can we, how can a Government dare reduce the income of people who already do not have enough? In terms of dollars, de-indexing old age pensions means that within five years, by 1990, a person living alone will lose something like 15 times $100, and of course married couples will lose twice as much. Now, Mr. Chairman, 1 do not think that our elders who worked stubbornly to build this country deserve to get so little consideration from their own Government, a Government they would have preferred to trust but in which they can have no confidence of any kind any more. Senior citizens now realize that they have been literally betrayed by the Progressive Conservative Government. That Government was committed to fully index old age pensions to the cost of living effective January 1st, 1985. The Government also made the commitment that no saving from program cuts would be used to reduce the deficit. That was the commitment this Government made to all Canadians. But with their plans to limit old age pension indexing, Canadians have realized that

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
this Government has taken them for a ride, that it did not tell the truth. They have realized that this Government has no concern for us Canadians, especially senior citizens.
Mr. Chairman, this simply cannot be allowed to go on unchallenged. We cannot accept that a government should make fun of us and of Canadians in such a way. Our elders are very much aware of this Government's scheme, they knew they were betrayed. In an interview with the Times-Transcript in Moncton, the Chairperson of the Federation of Senior Citizens has stated, and I quote:

The organization will start making waves from the Atlantic Ocean to the Pacific Ocean as it launches a campaign against a move which broke sacred trusts and sacred promises. We draw the line at sacred promises as internal peace and tranquility are very important at our age. We cannot understand how a political party could dare do such a thing.

What is worse, Mr. Chairman, how can the Minister of Finance and the government claim that our senior citizens are fully backing their proposal when in New Brunswick alone, 76,000 of them are against it. In fact, they object so strongly to the Government's proposal that they are ready to start a campaign against it.
Therefore it is wrong to claim that our senior citizens are in favour of such a change. Over the past weekend, Mr. Chairman, all hon. members representing New Brunswick ridings were invited to attend a meeting. I must say that all those who showed up were against the measures which the Government is contemplating. It goes without saying, therefore, that nobody in New Brunswick is in favour of this proposal.
Finally, Mr. Chairman, I must confess that 1 am somewhat perplexed when I see what is going on. To me no one can tamper with the indexing of Old Age Security Pensions. That is something Hon. Members opposite know as well as I do. Yet, I wonder why they took a chance with a proposal which they know would prove extremely unpopular with the Canadian people? Tell me why?
I could suggest a somewhat simple and obvious answer. One might be inclined to believe that the Government was setting a trap for us and the Canadian people in general. And we almost fell into that trap. On May 23rd, the Minister of Finance announced a series of unacceptable measures. One of the most unfair was of course the proposed desindexing of Old Age Security pensions. It was not long before people reacted, and rightly so. But while we are debating an issue on which the Government will have no choice but to back down, this session of Parliament is coming to an end, something for which the Government is delighted, because all the other pieces of legislation which are dangerous for us as Canadians and for our economy, will be quickly passed without any time left to discuss them.
In New Brunswick, beside the pension problem, there is a SI00 million cut in regional development, a $75 million cut at least in the transport sector which for us is of the utmost importance. Also a $25 million cut in the area of fisheries. Gas price increase will result in additional costs for all our small and medium sized businesses.
The reduction in provincial transfer payment, the freeze of unemployment insurance benefits, the imposition of a surtax, all these measures are just as important and just as unacceptable as the deindexing of pensions.
Mr. Chairman, judging from the breadth and scope of the debate on old age security pensions, it would seem that the Progressive Conservative Government will be busy this summer and will have to beg forgiveness from the Canadian public for having had the audacity to propose policies which go against the interests of Canadian citizens. The pension issue shows that the Canadian people know what they want, and what they want Mr. Chairman, is to have fair and equitable policies.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to make a few comments on the $18.2 billion borrowing authority requested by the Government. We have not received any satisfactory answers about what use will be made of this money.
At the same time that the Government is asking for $18.2 billion, it is coming forward with some very repressive measures. It is implementing cut-backs to senior citizens while it continues the pattern of Government waste. Cabinet Ministers are still using the private government jets to go to different parts of the country when they could use Air Canada.
It is reported in the newspaper that the Government will distribute a glossy External Affairs brochure featuring the Prime Minister in 18 pages of colour photography. The presidential style of the Prime Minister, the patronage appointments and this kind of Government waste contrasts rather sadly with the shabby way in which it is treating the senior citizens of this country. The mean spirited approach of the Government contrasts to some of the genuine improvements previous Parliaments have made to the living conditions of the seniors.
The Government's proposed 3 per cent cut-back in indexing of the Old Age Security program means that next year seniors will be receiving $100 less than they should have received if that indexing had continued. By 1990 they will have lost some $1,500 if deindexing continues.
A debate on this subject is taking place within the Conservative Party. Perhaps it is best typified by my friend, the Hon. Member for Victoria, who is a representative of many seniors in that community. He has had the. courage to speak up within his Party and say that he believes that what the Government is doing is wrong. I presume that he does this from a convergence
June 18, 1985

of two factors. First, he naturally is a man of compassion who can see what this measure will do to his constituents. Second, he is a man of reasonable intelligence who can read the political writing on the wall. The combination of these two factors, compassion and the ability to see what is happening politically, lead him to stand up and say that this is a proposal that is absolutely contrary to the wishes and best interests of his constituents and indeed all of Canada.
There is a saying in the scriptures that the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom. Perhaps Members opposite should begin to realize that a healthy respect for the wishes and views of the electorate might be the beginning of political wisdom.
It has only recently become clear that Members such as the Member for Victoria have lost this debate. It seems that the Minister of Finance is taking a hardened position and will not rescind the unpopular and regressive proposal to partially deindex Old Age Security. There might be a possibility of double indexing the Guaranteed Income Supplement. The Conservatives might try to pretend that this will solve the situation, but that is not the case. It may help those who are most adversely impacted at the very bottom of the scale-a great many Canadians are living in poverty-but it will not help those who are just above the poverty line and do not receive the Guaranteed Income Supplement. They have planned for their retirement, perhaps put some money aside and have another pension income to keep them slightly above that Guaranteed Income Supplement. The Government is mistaken if it believes it can solve this problem and get out of its political dilemma while retaining the cut-backs to the Old Age Security. Those Canadians who are just above receiving the Guaranteed Income Supplement will not be assisted and will be pushed further into poverty.
Our Party is making the case very strongly that the Government should not take a half step in retreat but should do the honourable thing, recognize that it has made a mistake and back right off. I am reminded of a song about Big Muddy. An American platoon sergeant who was leading his platoon down a path suddenly found himself in the middle of a swamp. Rather than having the intelligence to turn around, as the song depicts the historical example, "The big fool just kept right on marching". Similarly, rather than marching the Canadian people deeper into big muddy, the Conservative Government should have enough intelligence to recognize that it is taking us deeper into the swamp and it is time to turn around.
During last summer's campaign, the Prime Minister recognized and promised indexation of Old Age Security. The Minister of National Health and Welfare recognized that as a necessity last January. He said there was no need to make any alterations to our Old Age Security provision.
The Prime Minister, the Minister of National Health and Welfare and the Minister of Finance have given different explanations for this measure. First, they came up with the rather preposterous suggestion that seniors themselves favoured this move. They said that seniors recognized that there was a need for some sacrifice in order to cut the deficit and the country moving again and they were rushing forward

in support of this budgetary measure. Of course, when the Government was challenged to name one organization of senior citizens who supported this move, it was unable to do so.

Mr. Chairman, 1 am very happy to say a few words on Bill C-51 on the borrowing authority of the Government. I rise to speak today because I was quite surprised to realize that, if the Government now finds itself in such a situation, which represents an important political impasse in my opinion, it may be because it has forgotten the basic facts of politics. However, I do not want to make a political speech.
I simply want to point out to the Government that, in deciding to give a new direction to our economy, it might have wanted to operate like a private business. I know that many of my honourable colleagues on the other side come from the private sector and I give them credit for having tried to improve the economic situation in Canada. However, what I do not understand, Mr. Chairman, is that they would have used all kinds of tricks to suggest to all Canadian men and women that they were going to create another garden of Eden where everyone would be content, both the rich and the poor, where we would all be one happy family, the economy would prosper and everyone would be happy. This is why the Canadian voters placed their confidence in this Government and elected the party now in power with a large majority last September 4. I know that, on the hustings, people often say, without making formal promises, that they will implement programs with which the voters will be happy and which will make them feel better about living in this country, and this is often why the Canadian public votes as it does. The public made a choice, but unfortunately, as soon as this choice had been made, the Government brought down its first Budget and seemed to discredit itself in the eyes of the population and harmed its own credibility.
The present problem is a political impasse about the deindexing of old age security pensions. I think that the Government made a mistake. The reason is simple. During the campaign, the Members opposite said that everything would stay the same as before, but everything did not stay the same. This has eroded the confidence of people who have no other means to provide for themselves then the pension they have earned after many years and which has been adjusted to the cost of living as the consumer price index has increased.
1 would like to say that the indexation to cost of living is a choice that was made by the Canadian society. It was a choice because had it not been . . . And that may be the reason why we have such a huge deficit in Canada, because we have decided to compensate some members of the Canadian society who were retired, who could not earn any income any more and who were powerless in the face of inflation, we have decided to grant them this surplus in order for them to share the life enjoyed by all other Canadians.
So, in effect, Mr. Chairman, it is a choice that was made by the Canadian society as a whole. Obviously, the consumer price index has varied widely from one year to the other.

Presently, it is perhaps 5, 6 or 4 per cent. It may climb to 5 per cent at the end of this year. In any event, what is important, the bottom line is that we wanted to give some measure of protection to those whose sole income is their retirement income, to add a little supplement so that they can have perhaps a certain measure of comfort in the final stage of their life.
We are dealing here with people who are absolutely powerless, and that probably explains why, the other day, when 1 went to the Maison du Citoyen in Hull, where 300 or 400 old age people were celebrating with a banquet the closing of their annual Old Age Week, there was such an outcry against the government's attitude and the measures that have been taken in the Budget concerning the deindexing of the Old Age Security Pensions.
Mr. Chairman, I believe we do not have any right to hit members of the society who cannot defend themselves, and yet this is a political mistake because these people represent '0 per cent of the population. They are a political force we could use.
I am sure these 20 per cent will remember for a long time to come the attitude of this government, whatever that attitude may be, toward older people. I believe they will not forget easily and they will pass along to the future generations the memory of that injustsice that was perpetrated to them in this Budget.
It is a matter of basic, fundamental principle for the Canadian society.

From the outset, Mr. Chairman, I should like to correct immediately one aspect of this issue. Since the debate began this morning God knows how many times we heard the word deindexation, which is not mine.
What we in the Department of Finance came up with is indeed guaranteed indexation. It is a guarantee that anything over 3 per cent will be indexed. So please let the record show that what we are now advocating is a long-term measure which will guarantee that anything over 3 per cent will be compensated by the Government, and this is nothing like what happened in the past when people were worried about soaring inflation and had to stand the impact of an inflation increase of nearly 6 per cent in single year.
Secondly, in direct answer to the question: How much would the Government save in the fiscal year 1985-86? According to our advisers here it must be pointed out the savings would be for a three-month period only since the measure would be in force as of January 1. Once in force we would have to include the 3 per cent in absolute figures while keeping in mind as well this statement taken from the Budget speech: "The Government will review the adequancy of payments in light of future circumstances and will increase them as resources permit". So we are going to give the basic 3 per cent, but there is more than that because our policy will be to help those who need most rather than try to help everybody. In answer to the question then, savings during the fiscal year 1985-86 would not amount to much more than $15 million, but they would rise to some $245 million for the fiscal year 1986-87.

However, I do not want to go into that again today. The Parliamentary Secretary knows full well that a limited program was implemented because inflation had been rampant for three, four or five years. Under a rationalization program, workers were asked to restrict their salary increases to 6 and 5 per cent, while the indexation of tax tables were restricted to 6 and 5 per cent and a ceiling of 6 and 5 per cent was put on everything. It is all very well for the Minister or the Parliamentary Secretary to say that if conditions improve, old age security pensions will be increased and more money will be paid. But that is not what we are being told at present. We are told that the first 3 per cent of the OAS indexing will be lost. And if inflation exceeds 3 per cent, of course, only that part will be covered. I do not want to complicate matters and try to suggest that pensions are cut by 3 per cent, but future indexing will be restricted. As far as I am concerned I don't want to fight tooth and nail over this, but if we were to plug . .. and mind you, we would not have to plug too many loopholes to find $15 million out of $300 million. support that amendment. If it has seen fit to reduce the benefits to our senior citizens by 3 per cent in January, it should in fairness cut its own expenditures in a similar way.
As 1 was walking into the House of Commons tonight from a committee meeting in the West Block 1 saw the fleet of brand new vehicles lined up, with their engines idling, waiting for their $100,000 people to arrive. Surely, if this Government and the Cabinet have seen fit to reduce the purchasing power of the senior citizens by 3 per cent in January, they would not mind tightening up their belts a little and reducing Government expenditures.
The Prime Minister increased his office operation by, 1 believe, 54 per cent in this fiscal year. 1 am sure he would not mind cutting back that extra $2 million by 3 per cent. I am sure he would not mind cutting back by 3 per cent his staff which already has been increased by 33 per cent. He is asking the senior citizens to do that. 1 am sure he wants to be fair and equitable. He promised to do all these things. I am surprised that the Government is holding up the vote on this amendment because I am sure it wants to be fair to our senior citizens.
I believe as we look down the pipe over a period of four years or five years, we see exactly how this Government proposes to operate; that is by stealth, misrepresentation, and by not levelling with the Canadian people. When the Government put out the Estimates of Government revenues and expenditures it was only for 1985-86. But if we project those costs over a long period of time, taking 3 per cent less this year, 3 per cent less next year, and so on, not only to the indexation of the income tax levels but to the standard personal exemptions, and we do that as well to senior citizens pensions, we sort of get them both coming and going.
For instance, let us look at the benefits to the rich, the powerful and the mighty in this country. We see that the surtax only applies for 1985-86 and 1986-87. That is just a little over 18 months. Let us look at the special tax on the banks. It likewise only applies over a very short period of time, amounting to something like $10 million this year in surtax and $100 million next year. We see that the rich and the powerful pay a surtax, but for perhaps only 18 months.
If we look at the low and moderate income groups we see their benefits cut off year after year. Let us look at the modification to the personal income tax scale. It only amounts to $80 million this year, but by 1990-1991 the low and moderate income families will be paying $4,360 billion a year more in personal income tax. I know that Hon. Members opposite do not like to hear this because when they put out the Budget they did not bother showing what the long-term impact would be of the deindexation of the personal levels of income tax.
Let us look at the impact on the Registered Home Ownership Savings Program. It hits at young families and young couples. I met with a young couple in Toronto two weeks ago who told me they were paying $650 a month for rent. They said if they could get the down payment, such as the RHOSP would provide, they would be able to purchase a home by paying only another $150 a month. But this Budget does away
Borrowing Authority Act
with that program, which means that thousands of young couples who might have been able to put aside the down payment for a home using the RHOSP Program will not now be able to do so.
I cannot, for the life of me, understand why when the Minister of Finance was releasing those funds which are held in the RHOSP Program, he did not allow them to be taken out this year and invested in a home, in furnishings or in major appliances. The people I have talked to have told me that they would just roll it over into another fund. So even if those funds are released without taxation this year, they will not be generating any jobs related to major consumer goods, and they will not be providing the down payments for a home.
If we look at the rest of the projections over a five-year period we see that the loss, because of the capital gains tax exemption, jumps from $300 million this year to $1.25 billion by 1990-91. The Minister has portrayed this as a job creation scheme. If he really wanted it to be that, rather than a valentine to his friends on Bay Street in high income brackets, it seems to me that he would have made a provision whereby the capital gains would be invested in Canadian business and farms rather than in anything from a condo in Florida to art and all kinds of things. Clearly what will happen is that people who have a capital gain of $500,000, because most of them will be in a high income bracket, will save themselves $125,000 with no benefit to the country. Surely what we want is a fair tax regime to encourage development and provide jobs.
The elimination of the PGRT will save the multinational oil companies $124 million this year, and $2,449 billion by 1990. That is rather interesting because the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources outlined several weeks ago about seven major projects which she saw going ahead. I have forgotten the exact number of jobs created in the development stage of projects like Venture and Hibernia, but the total number of permanent jobs for those seven major projects was something like 31. We hear of small Canadian owned companies who are afraid of being taken over by these rich multinationals. Not only have they had the PGRT removed with no effective monitoring system to see that those funds are reinvested, but they gain as well because the value of the oil they have in the ground will increase by some $800 million this year. We are seeing a massive transfer from the poor, the middle-income earners, and senior citizens to the rich, the powerful, and the multinationals. How can the Government justify that?
Last fall in his Economic Statement the Minister of Finance made a great thing of the Government's campaign promise to reduce the excise tax on gasoline for farmers and primary producers. It was reduced by some 20 cents a gallon, but in the Budget it was increased by 9 cents a gallon. The Government realized that excise tax would be harmful to the tourist industry so it does not take effect until early September, but that is the time when the harvest in western Canada is getting into full swing. The people in the West are appalled. They cannot understand the duplicity of the Government in remov-

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
ing the tax last fall and then reimposing it when the harvest is really beginning. In western Canada it is being described as the harvest tax. Add to that the fact that the Government, with no exemption that I have been able to find for farmers and primary producers, will reimpose a sales tax January 1 on energy costs, indeed on all farm input costs. So we see a number of items in the Budget which are very harmful to Canadian agriculture.
The tobacco industry is suffering tremendously and the Government has imposed an additional tax of 25 cents on a package of cigarettes. The tobacco farmers say that will be very harmful. A tax levy of some 2 per cent on alcohol has drawn a violent reaction from the grape and wine industry in the Niagara area and other parts of our country. As well, the Government has said it will be reducing the budget of the Department of Agriculture by $50 million a year over the next five years. Given a budget of about $1.25 billion, a cut of $250 million is very significant.
The Budget does not say specifically where those cuts will be. They may be in crop insurance. The Government may ask the provinces to put up half the crop insurance premiums, or a third, along with the federal Government and producers. The cuts may be in transportation assistance or agricultural research. That is not clear, but if you look at the Budget papers it is clear there will be a cut of $50 million a year. Perhaps the cut will be in the milk stabilization program, a program which not only provides assistance to our agricultural producers, but also acts as a unifying or cohesive force to help keep them in business.
Will the Parliamentary Secretary indicate if the budget of the Department of Agriculture will be frozen at its present level, less the $50 million, or will it increase 3 per cent or 4 per cent, less the $50 million? What effect will reducing the borrowing authority in line with the reduction being applied to senior citizens have on the budget of the Department of Agriculture?
The Ontario Federation of Agriculture met on June 6 at a special directors meeting in Toronto. Not only did the regular table officers of the federation attend, but the county directors and county presidents were there as well. It was one of the largest emergent meetings they had at which to consider exactly what to do in response to the Budget.
They passed a resolution at that meeting which Hon. Members should read because I know they are very concerned about the plight of farmers in the country. Tomorrow they will hold a special emergency meeting to plan the strategy for coping with the cut-backs which the Government has made in the agricultural budget and how to deal with the disincentives and lack of action in the Budget presented by the Government.
During the election campaign, the Government promised to introduce an agri-bond program. Obviously the Minister of Finance did not support that program because he was demonstrably against an agri-bond program in his special White Paper on taxation issues in agriculture. He was also
against any concessions on Section 31 of the Income Tax Act and changes in the capital gains tax. While he recognized the capital gains provision for farmers in his Budget, he took no action with respect to the agri-bond program. That is regrettable because the Finance committee made a strong presentation for a long term agri-bond program with low interest rates.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, 1 am delighted to be able to speak on this amendment. Frankly, it has been presented in order to send a strong message to the Government because, in spite of strong protests, representations and pleadings from millions of senior citizens and Canadians generally as well as Members of the Official Opposition and the other Opposition Party in the House, the Government has refused to listen. It has acted in an arrogant and stubborn manner by insisting that it will proceed with the Budget measure to deindex senior citizens pensions and not allow any adjustment for inflation below 3 per cent.
From time to time. Government spokesmen hint that something may be done at some future date to respond to the quite justified concerns over the deindexing proposal in the Budget. However, the Government does not take a consistent line. The Prime Minister speaks in a soft, cajoling, conciliatory manner, suggesting that he understands the concerns of seniors and there is nothing to worry about because action will be taken to respond to those concerns. However, when the Minister of Finance speaks about the same subject, his tone is very different. It is harsh and stubborn, indicating a closed and arrogant mind when it comes to this crucial subject of such great concern to millions of senior citizens and millions of Canadians generally.
All we had to do to confirm this point was listen to the Minister of Finance during Question Period today when he talked about the need to reduce the deficit above all. He talked about the need for senior citizens to bear what we consider to be an unfair and unnecessary share of the burden to reduce that deficit.
It was as if nothing had been said and nothing had happened since the night the Budget had been presented. Anybody who had been listening at all and had not been away on another planet, in his mind if not in reality, would have known that there had been a growing feeling of outrage on the part of Canada's senior citizens and Canadians generally when they recognized what that cold, arrogant and unfeeling Government was fully intending to do in its Budget of May 23 when it talked about removing the indexing of senior citizens' pensions for all inflationary increases in the cost of living below 3 per cent.
How can anyone take anything the Government says seriously about the Budget in general, or about this provision to cut the indexing of senior citizens' pensions in particular, when it is talking out of both sides of its collective mouth? On the one hand there is the soft cajoling, honeyed, yet not credible words of the Prime Minister and, on the other, the tough.
June 18, 1985

arrogant, unfeeling words of the Minister of Finance in the House today. I suggest that those latter words represent the real views, opinions and decisions of that cold and unfeeling Government. That is why the Budget not only deserves to be rejected but that the amendment before the committee deserves to be strongly supported.
The Minister of Finance continues to claim, as he did in the House during Question Period today, that there is no change being made to the Old Age Security pension. He says that if the Budget is adopted in the form in which it has been presented to the House, senior citizens will continue to receive cheques at face value, in amounts that will not be in any way less than face value amounts of those cheques now. No one is denying or debating that point. We are saying on behalf of millions of senior citizens and senior citizens are saying themselves that the sneaky, unfair provision to cut indexing in the Budget will cut the purchasing power-

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT

speechtext: Not necessarily.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
On and on in perpetuity. We must stand up for the Canadian people and send a message to this arrogant and unfeeling Government through the amendment before the committee and through fighting as hard as we can against an arrogant and unfeeling Budget presented by an arrogant and unfeeling Government.
Frankly, even the Minister of Finance, when he is not in the House, is willing to admit that the provision in the Budget to cut the indexation of the pensions of senior citizens will in fact harm seniors by cutting their purchasing power. In fact, the following was reported today in The Toronto Star about the Minister of Finance when he was in Halifax:
And Wilson later agreed with reporters' suggestions that there will be a decrease in the "real dollar value" of pensions.
No matter what the Minister of Finance tries to say in the House to defend his indefensible Budget, deep down he knows what is wrong with that part of the Budget dealing with the pensions of senior citizens. While he is not yet ready to admit it to the House, where he should admit it first, he admitted it when faced with this reality from reporters in Halifax yesterday.
The Minister of Finance and other government spokesmen keep saying that the only reason senior citizens are protesting the deindexing provision of the Budget is because of the scare tactics of the Opposition, that the seniors have been stirred up by the scare tactics of the Opposition.
The Government is insulting the intelligence and common sense of our senior citizens. They are able to analyse proposals in this Budget as well as anyone. They are able to make up
Borrowing Authority Act
their own minds about what is wrong with the Budget in general and about what it says when it comes to pensions of senior citizens in particular. Whether it is the Minister of Finance, the Deputy Prime Minister, the Prime Minister or anyone on the government side of the House, when it comes to them saying that senior citizens are only upset about the Budget because of the scare tactics of the Opposition, all they are saying is that they do not attribute enough intelligence and common sense to our senior citizens to think for themselves and make up their own minds. That is an insult to our senior citizens which should be placed on the record. 1 am sure it will be held against this arrogant and unfeeling Government for a long time to come.
To demonstrate that senior citizens are quite capable of thinking for themselves and making up their own minds about what is wrong with the Budget, I refer the Committee to a press release dated June 13 and issued by Mrs. Yhetta Gold, President of the National Advisory Council on Aging. According to the press release, Mrs. Gold sent a letter to the Minister of National Health and Welfare, from which I want to quote some relevant extracts as set forth in the press release. In her letter she said:
The May 23 Budget... has stimulated seniors to joint together to lobby and advocate on their own behalf. Seniors are saying "Listen to me" to Government.
The tragedy is that the Government is refusing to listen. This is why we have to send a message, on behalf of seniors, to this arrogant and unfeeling Government through the amendment which we presented to the Committee on this Borrowing Authority Bill. In part the press release goes on to state:
Commenting on her letter, Mrs. Gold indicated that "deindexing has not only brought seniors together but also many other Canadians including youth and business groups".
The press release continues by referring to the response of seniors to the May 23 Budget and "their belief that they should not be penalized any more than the general public". Also it states:
NACA is encouraged by the response of seniors and their associations and is sure that seniors will continue their efforts-
Another part of the press release reads:
The letter to Mr. Epp refers to other effects of deindexing. According to the Council "it will provide a short-term saving in exchange for a long-term loss. The stress associated with a tighter and tighter budget will take its toll. More and more senior Canadians will find it difficult to cope with a deteriorating physical, mental and social condition. In time, expenditures for other types of care will limit the savings due to deindexing", according to the Council.
I have quoted from a letter which was sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare by the President of NACA, the official body established by government to advise government on the needs and concerns of the aging. This demonstrates that what government spokesmen are saying, to the effect that it is only the scare tactics of the Opposition which are stirring up senior citizens, is absolutely wrong, inaccurate and downright false. The letter sent by Mrs. Gold to the Minister shows very clearly that the National Advisory Council on Aging, the senior advisory body speaking for senior citizens, has analysed the government Budget and what it said about pensions. It has figured out for itself, on behalf of senior

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
citizens, that the Budget will reduce the purchasing powers of old age pensioners in ways which will be very harmful to senior citizens, not only now but for a long time to come.
1 also draw to the attention of the Committee another very important point which was made in this June 13 press release by NACA. It reads:
NACA also believes that pre-retirees, the 60 to 64 age group (1.1 million Canadians with an average income of less than $17,000) will be hurt by deindexing OAS. "Many will have to modify drastically their retirement plans and save more to compensate for their loss of income, or delay their retirement", said Mrs. Gold. "The first is not conducive to economic growth and the latter will have Canadians even more anxious about jobs."
These are the words of the President of the non-political and non-partisan National Advisory Council on Aging.
If the Government is not yet ready to listen to what the Official Opposition says about this, surely it will listen to the National Advisory Council on Aging. If it is not ready to listen to NACA, then it is clear why, as I have already said, we have to send a message to the Government on behalf of senior citizens and all Canadians through the amendment before the Committee, that the Budget in general is wrong and in particular it is wrong when it wants to cut the purchasing power of pensions for older Canadians.
There are many other reasons to send a message to the Government through this amendment. The Minister of Finance continues to say that no changes will be made to the Old Age Security pension. If that is correct, why do the budget documents attribute hundreds of millions of dollars in savings from what the Budget says about deindexing Old Age Security pensions, savings which the Government intends to use to reduce the deficit? If everything remains the same, from where will the savings come which the Government says it will get from the Old Age Security system to reduce the deficit?
The truth of the matter is that the Government is changing the Old Age Security system. If that were not the case, it would not have those savings to reduce the deficit. What is even more shameful about what the Government is trying to do in this Budget, in a sneaky and surreptitious fashion, is that in its official Blue Paper of last January, it said that it would not make any changes to the present Old Age Security system. In that Blue Paper, the Government said that the present system was working well and did not require any changes. Let us not let the Government get away with trying to explain the unexplainable, when it tries to justify its Budget and the drop in purchasing power as a result of the deindexation it wants to make to Old Age Security pensions, by saying that it has suddenly discovered that the deficit is so large that it had to do something, that it had to put an extra burden on older Canadians.
The fact is that when that Blue Paper came out, the Government had already been in office for many months. It already had full access to the books of the Government and knew what the financial position of the Government was then and what it was going to be. In its Blue Paper it said that the present system of Old Age Security pensions was working well,
that if there were to be any changes, they would be only to improve pensions and the social security system, and that any savings would never, never be used to reduce the deficit.
This Budget shows us how much we can believe what the Government says.
