speechtext:
The Government ought to be ashamed of itself for pressing ahead with this Budget and for having this borrowing authority Bill before the House. Through the amendment before this Committee we must send a message to this cold, arrogant and unfeeling Government.
In order to try to defend the indefensible and justify the unjustifiable, the Minister of Finance and government spokespersons say that this Budget is going to create jobs.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext: Hear, hear! Good idea.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Members on the other side of the House say "Hear, hear. Good idea". Yes, it is a good idea, but will someone explain to me why there are no forecasts whatsoever in this Budget of the number of jobs it is supposed to create? Where are the forecasts of jobs? There are no forecasts, but there is something else in the Budget which shows what the Government really thinks the Budget is going to do with regard to jobs. The Budget has forecasts about economic growth. The Budget says that while economic growth in the last year of Liberal government was 4.7 per cent, the results of Tory economics would be that in two years that level of growth would be cut in half.
How can hundreds of thousands of jobs be created as a result of this indefensible Budget if, at the same time, that Budget is going to cut economic growth in half? That is Tory economics. That is not job creation. That is not a Budget which helps Canada. In their indefensible budget documents, the Conservatives themselves are admitting that this Budget will hurt the economy and cut jobs. If I am wrong in this, Mr. Chairman, let the Minister of Finance, who is cowering in the back row, come forward and produce the figures of his Department, which he did not have the courage to put in his Budget, which show how many jobs his Budget is going to create and explain how his Budget is going to create any jobs if its result is to cut economic growth in half.
He cannot do that because he knows that even Tory economics will not create hundreds of thousands of jobs with a rate of growth which is less than half of what it was in the last year of Liberal Government.
On behalf of senior citizens and all Canadians, I say that this arrogant, unfeeling Government needs to get the message that it is wrong, wrong, wrong. It is unfair, cruel, and heartless in what it is trying to do through its Budget to senior citizens and middle and lower income Canadians generally. If the Government does not receive the message through this amendment, we will continue to fight long and hard on behalf of Canadians because the Government is not going to do it and Canadians have already started to catch on.

speechtext: All socialists, my goodness, Mr. Chairman. 1 will not give a long list of columnists who have been saying the same thing. However, 1 will quote from Mr. Jeffrey Simpson who writes regularly in The Globe and Mail.

speechtext: Which is quite a radical paper.

subtopic: BORROWING AUTHORITY ACT, 1985-86 (No. 2) MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
That is quite a radical paper, as my hon. friend from Winnipeg North says. In The Globe and Mail, our effort at a national newspaper, Mr. Simpson, who is a reputed columnist, said the following:
In Sherbrooke, Quebec, on July 26, 1984, Brian Mulroney promised unequivocally to "reinstate complete indexing of Old Age Pensions to the actual cost of living, as of January 1, 1985.
People who heard those comments would have believed that the Prime Minister was saying that when the Conservatives became the Government they would reindex pensions to their full level. That is what he said and I suspect that is what people would believe. The Prime Minister said:
Senior citizens are often isolated, poor and in a crippling state of dependence. Recent statistics indicate that more than 60 per cent of women and 40 per cent of men over the age of 65 who live alone have incomes that are below the poverty line.
The Prime Minister was pointing out, as he should, the plight in which the elderly of Canada find themselves. The Prime Minister went on to say:
The position of senior citizens in our society has slipped drastically in recent years.
That means that the purchasing power and disposable income of senior citizens had eroded over the years and that conditions were worsening for them. The article goes on:
Allan McKinnon, a former Tory defence minister ... says there is anger and concern about deindexing of pensions. Alan Redway, whose York East riding is full of seniors, believes the Government must "review the issue".
Borrowing Authority Act
We have heard from a number of Conservative Members who, when caught by a reporter at a weak moment, said that they were getting mail on this matter and wanted to register their deep concern. We have been debating this issue for two days trying to find ways and means of approving this $18 billion borrowing authority. We have been asking questions and I do not think it is unreasonable to expect somebody from the government benches to stand and say that they really think that hammering senior citizens and slashing their pensions is a good idea.
I am reminded of a Question Period not long ago when the Minister of National Health and Welfare was asked if he could name a single individual who supported the Government's position, let alone a single group. He hummed and hawed and said that he thought he could, then went on to talk his way out of that question.
The Prime Minister of Canada has said that senior citizens are isolated poor who are in a crippling state of dependence. He has also said that their situation in society has slipped drastically in recent years and is slipping even further. Then the first chance the Government gets to provide leadership- and I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance is here- the Government indicates that the problems of senior citizens, the problems with deindexation and the problems it had identified in the election campaign are going to be ignored.
The Government decided that it was going to ignore the critical problems. Since it wanted to give tax breaks to the 4 per cent of tax filers who file capital gains on the first $500,000 of income from capital gains, it needed to come up with the money some place, so it decided to hammer the 10 per cent of Canadians who are senior citizens. This is not my analysis but is the point that is made by Jeffrey Simpson. He has said that if the 4 per cent is put against the 10 per cent of the population, there is a political problem.
Every single Member opposite knows that there is a political problem in his or her constituency. I would like to think that there is a great deal of pressure within the Conservative caucus to change the mind of the Minister of Finance on this particular issue.
The Minister of Finance and his caucus colleagues were saying that we all have to suffer a little bit and that it is reasonable to ask senior citizens, most of whom live below the poverty line, to take a 3 per cent cut in their disposable income over the next number of years. To be more accurate, that means that by the year 1990-91, senior citizens will have $1.6 billion taken from their pockets in one year. Between now and then, that adds up to $6.6 billion that we will take away from senior citizens.
Jeffrey Simpson goes on to describe an interesting balance. After all, the Minister of Finance said that there was justice and that he had weighed the situation very carefully. However, 1990, the year the $1.6 billion will be taken from the pockets of seniors, is also the year when that 4 per cent of the people who file capital gains will receive $1.25 billion. In other words,

June 18, 1985
Borrowing Authority Act
we are taking from the poorest citizens of Canada to give to the most wealthy citizens of Canada. At least that is the analysis as I see it, and I trust some of my colleagues opposite will correct me if I am wrong.
The Government is requesting that we cut the income of seniors by 3 per cent, so it is not unreasonable to ask the Government to cut 3 per cent from its borrowing authority. That is the motion we are debating at the moment. The Minister of Finance has said that we should be passing this $18 billion borrowing authority quickly so that the Government can get on with doing the job. Doing the job means a number of things. As the Minister of Finance has indicated time and time again, doing the job means creating jobs. He has said that the Budget he introduced on May 23 will create jobs. Let us take a look a what some analysts have to say about that. Again, I am not referring to a good NDP source but to a post-Budget survey done by the Canada Permanent Trust Company.
The Canada Permanent Trust Company contacted a wide variety of business economists. 1 would point out that these are business economists and not academic economists. They are people who make their living examining the Canadian economy and advising their clients on what is happening in terms of future economic development.
Interestingly enough, Canada Permanent found that none of the forecasters agree that the Minister of Finance's promise of greater job creation will succeed. Not one single business economist that was commissioned by the Canada Permanent Trust Company could find anyone who felt that the Minister of Finance's promise of greater job creation would succeed. As a matter of fact, 20 per cent of those business economists expected that the jobless rate would be higher than it had been before the Budget. That is a very telling comment because one of the reasons for the Government asking senior citizens to bleed a little bit and one of the reasons for the Government to slap user-fees on a whole variety of things and to raise sales taxes and taxes on confectioneries is because it will create jobs. Yet business economists, people who make their living by predicting the implications of the Budget, say that this will not take place and that as a matter of fact the situation will worsen.
Let us take a look at what else the economists have had to say. Seventy-six per cent of those business economists who were surveyed said that they are unlikely to alter their projections of real growth this year because of the Budget. In other words, 76 per cent of them felt that they had no reason to change the projections of growth or lack of it as a result of the Budget. That is very interesting, Mr. Chairman.
As well, the economists felt that the new tax measures will drastically reduce the spending power of the average Canadian. I think that this is rather important because the Government has asked us to give enhusiastic endorsement to its request to borrow $18.2 billion while we are being told that the small and medium-sized business sectors are falling all over themselves in their enthusiasm to create jobs. Probably everyone in this House believes that the small and medium-sized
business sectors would like to expand operations, but to do that, they require one thing: they require a population that has the confidence and the wherewithal to purchase whatever it is that is being produced, whether it be a good or a service.
The Budget that was introduced on May 23, along with the November statement made by the Minister of Finance, takes away from every family in Canada $1,000 of disposable income. As well, over the next five years, every single senior citizen in Canada will lose $1,500 from his or her disposable income. It does not take much imagination to figure this out. I hope that Members opposite will understand what 1 am about to say.
When so much disposable income is taken away at the same time as people are being asked to buy more in order to assist small business, the logic breaks down somewhere in that process. One cannot expect businesses to expand if people are not prepared to purchase goods or services, yet that is what the Government expects will happen. I suspect that is why the business economists to which I referred a moment ago did not agree that the Minister of Finance's promise of greater job creation will succeed.
I ask Hon. Members opposite who feel that the incentive of capital gains tax avoidance will encourage job creation and expansion to tell me about any Government in the world that has introduced a similar policy that has resulted in net economic expansion and job creation. I do not think Hon. Members could find a successful example of that. It is good in theory but in actual fact, I do not think that it has ever occurred. I challenge Hon. Members opposite to correct me on that assumption if I am wrong.
I would like to end my comments today by indicating why we as New Democrats are less than enthusiastic about giving carte blanche approval to the Government so that it may borrow $18.2 billion and why we are less than enthusiastic about the Budget that was introduced by the Minister of Finance.
A few days ago my colleague from Essex-Windsor gave the House a history lesson. For Members who were not present on that day, I would like to repeat that lesson. He recalled an election campaign which was waged against an arrogant Liberal Government. At the time there was a decline in productivity, a decline in the country's production and a dramatic increase in unemployment. People said that the situation had to change and that the arrogant Liberal Government had to go.
The Tories spoke of optimism, hope, a better Canada and a new era. In Regina, the Leader of the Conservative Party said: "This is a new country. There is no excuse for unemployment in Canada if the Government does its duty." In Moncton, New Brunswick, he said: "The Conservative Party is going to find work for all who are willing to work or perish in the attempt, and take such steps as will end the tragic conditions of unemployment and bring prosperity to the country as a whole." During that election campaign the Conservative
June 18, 1985

Leader said: "I promise to end unemployment in Canada." The Tories were swept into power. The Tories were elected on those promises, with an overwhelming majority.
A Budget was brought down shortly thereafter. The Minister of Trade and Commerce, Mr. Stevens, said that the Budget was wise and courageous. The Budget included major cutbacks in government services. It included reductions in agricultural services to western, central and eastern Canada. It imposed additional taxation on all people of Canada. It imposed new taxes through increases in the sales tax, increases on import duties and what were then called nuisance taxes. Those whose incomes were $10,000 a year saw their taxes increase by 53 per cent as a result of the Budget. However, if a person's income was $1 million, their taxes only increased by 31 per cent. At that time, Social Democrats stood up in the House and said that the millionaires had been very gently dealt with by the Minister of Finance.
That was the election campaign of 1930. The promise of tens of thousands of jobs was made by R. B. Bennett. The Budget was brought down by the Hon. Henry Stevens in 1932. Canadian people got a shot at that Conservative Government in 1935. They realized the disastrous results of the Budget. They knew that the promises which had been made in the 1930 election campaign were empty promises. That Government did not deliver.
The point is that it is nothing new. The rhetoric is the same. The Budget is the same. It is R. B. Bennett all over again. We know how successful those practices were at that time. Mr. Chairman, I see my colleagues opposite questioning some of the comments I have made. Will one Member opposite stand and explain how this Budget is different from the one brought in by R. B. Bennett in 1932? Can they explain how this Budget was different from the major thrust of the 1932 Budget? Can they explain how the promises which were made by the Conservatives in 1932 were any different in principle, thrust, or even words, from the Budget of 1985?
I suspect that is the reason why people today cannot take these people too seriously. They have seen it before. I would encourage people to read what happened during the election campaign of 1930 and the subsequent years until the next election in 1935. They will find that the times and approaches of the Conservative Government then were no different from the times and approaches of the Conservative Government today. That is why we find this Bill inappropriate. This is not the kind of borrowing authority which results in enthusiastic endorsement by members of the New Democratic Party.

Mr. Chairman, I welcome this opportunity to speak to the amendment to Bill C-51, because the Budget brought down on May 23 of this year was supposed to emphasize employment, according to the slogans used by the Progressive Conservative Party during the election campaign last summer: 'Job, jobs, jobs.*
Although the Conservative Government stated that its first priority was employment, it has failed to come up with a real strategy. It hopes that tax deductions, including the tax exemption on $500,000 in capital gains, will be an incentive for people to invest and for businesses to create jobs. This is speculative, to say the least.
The most controversial proposal in the Budget is of course de-indexation of Old Age Security pensions. Mr. Chairman, this is a generation that lived through the Depression and World War II, a generation that raised large families and worked at a time when there was no such thing as retirement plan. I think it is obscene to ask a generation that has suffered so much to make even more sacrifices, when the Government gives the wealthy in our society over half a million dollars in tax exemptions.
I would like to say a few words about this tax measure. The proposition that jobs can be created by offering a tax exemption worth $500,000 is very speculative indeed, and I am not alone in holding this view. A number of independent observers think so too. The day after the Budget, one of our economic experts wrote in the press that the Government had failed both to reduce the deficit and reduce unemployment. Mr. Alain Dubuc, whose political objectivity and professional integrity are without question, said in his article that the measures introduced to benefit business would not necessarily bring about an increase in the number of jobs. For instance, eliminating the tax on $500,000 in capital gains may also encourage the purchase and sale of stocks and real estate, without creating a single job. The Government assumes that the Budget will create jobs after creating a climate of confidence. However, this is still speculative rather than a sure thing. That being said, until those jobs are created, if they ever are, the middle class is seeing the erosion of its purchasing power.
Mr. Chairman, yesterday in Baie Comeau, the Prime Minister accused the Liberal Party of scaring senior citizens. Mr. Chairman, the Prime Minister is trying to put the blame on the Liberal Party for causing anxiety among the elderly. The Liberals are not the only ones who are worried about our senior citizens. Read the papers, Mr. Chairman, listen to what senior citizens' organizations are saying and look at the cartoons in the papers. Did you see the cartoon in the Telegraph Journal on June 4? It shows the Prime Minister pushing a couple of senior citizens, while he is saying: "Sure the budget is tough enough on some citizens, but we must concern ourselves with those voters who will be around next election."

June 18, 1985
The cartoon in the Toronto Star of June 10 shows a senior citizen being tripped. These are not figments of the Liberal Party's imagination, Mr. Chairman. The Conservative Government is following a right-wing policy and is putting all its money on private enterprise. It is determined to reduce the size of Government. It is true that everywhere in the Western world people are questioning the influence of the welfare state and what the degree of Government involvement should be in the economy, but more and more people are starting to think that a mixed economy where the state still has a substantial involvement remains the ideal solution for a country like Canada. The Conservative Government has decided to abdicate its responsibilities in this respect.
Totally oblivious to the fact that we are in a democracy, the Minister of Finance stated in his Budget presentation that for too long, and I am quoting, Mr. Chairman, the Government decided what was good for Canadians. It set priorities, steered activities and subsidized efforts.
Well, Mr. Chairman, was it not the role of a democratically elected Government? I should like to recall a few facts concerning senior citizens, women and poverty. Poverty is the lot of women, particularly elderly women. Being both a woman and elderly is a ticket to poverty in Canada. The odds that an elderly woman will have a low income are about 66 per cent and she has the dubious honour of being poor for a longer time since, on average, she lives seven years longer than her husband.
If being both a woman and elderly is a ticket to poverty, being an elderly woman and a widow is a sure guarantee. More than 50 per cent of married women expect to be widows some day, and 70 per cent of widows and single women aged 70 or more live in poverty. As a rule, a widow does not get anything out of the retirement plan of her husband's employer and is entitled only to limited benefits under the Canada Pension Plan and the Quebec Pension Plan. The situation is not the same for her husband-he continues to get the same pension even after his wife has died.
The income to which a widow is entitled after the death of her husband is less than 30 per cent of their previous income as a couple, and should a widow remarry she almost invariably loses the benefits she might have otherwise. Three out of five women over 65 and four out of five women over 75 are single, widows or divorced.
Mr. Chairman, these few facts are a reminder that women make up most of the elderly group and that they are more directly affected by deindexation. Women have long since been waiting for the day when Canadian society will put them on the same footing as men. Elderly women have long since been waiting for the day when they will be able to live in complete dignity rather than live off social assistance. In my opinion, therefore, pension deindexation is unacceptable to an elderly person since it flies in the face of the most basic principles of
Borrowing Authority Act
social justice. Indeed, Mr. Chairman, what justice is there in reducing from one year to the next the purchasing power of a group of people who are among the most needy in our society? In my opinion, this is an inhumane measure which denies the fine principles contained in the speeches made by the Prime Minister during his election campaign.
I remember the solemn promises made by the Hon. Member for Baie Comeau (Mr. Mulroney) last summer. First, he was to re-establish full cost of living indexing of old age security pensions from January 1, 1985, and he also said that, as soon as its financial position would allow it, the government would provide greater financial assistance to single senior citizens still living below the poverty line, that the New Horizons program would be maintained and that it would be adequately funded. In his usual low and solemn voice, which he uses to try to show how serious his comments are, the Right Hon. Prime Minister therefore made specific promises to senior citizens. From now on, Mr. Chairman, we should perhaps become suspicious when the Prime Minister lowers his voice and speaks slowly. The solemnity of his voice is not proportional to the priority he gives an issue, contrary to what he is always trying to make Canadians believe.
The deindexing of senior citizens' pensions is unacceptable. Even the Prime Minister heard this yesterday evening in Baie Comeau, and he did not succeed in convincing anyone. I therefore believe that it is more than time for him to retreat. It is time to reassure senior citizens and tell them that deindexing will not happen.

Mr. Chairman, I would like to speak on this debate because I have heard so much nonsense from the government benches that I cannot remain silent. Our Party is not opposed to borrowing. Our Party is not as frightened of the deficit as the Conservative Party which now forms the Government. We support deficits and we support borrowing if they are required for reasons which make sense, if they are required to help people who need help and if they provide jobs. We cannot support a borrowing Bill which takes from those who are poor and old and gives to those who already have more than anyone else.
The Government is proposing to take $1.6 billion from the retired people of Canada to give almost all of it, $ 1.4 billion, to those in the top income levels of the country. That we cannot support. There is nothing which has made me more angry than to hear Conservative Members of Parliament here in the House of Commons and outside say that there is no real concern among the retired people of this country, that they understand what the Government is doing and are prepared to take their share of the burden in getting the country moving in
June 18, 1985

the right direction. They say that all the fuss we hear is caused by the misinformation given to senior citizens by members of the Opposition. That tells me that Conservative Members of Parliament, beginning with the Prime Minister and the Minister of Finance, have contempt for senior citizens. They believe that senior citizens are stupid.
Government Members believe that even though what the Government is proposing is good and necessary, somehow those terrible people in the Opposition have fooled and befuddled senior citizens so that they are expressing opposition to what the Government proposes even though what the Government proposes is good and should really be supported. They are really saying about senior citizens that not only are they old and poor but they are stupid. They are not stupid. They understand what is going on and they have reacted in a way which I have not seen before in almost 40 years of political life. 1 have never seen such unanimous opposition to a proposal made by any Government, federal or provincial, as I have seen expressed in the last few days and weeks to the proposal in the Budget designed to reduce the income of senior citizens by 3 per cent per year beginning in January 1986.
I do not know how the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance came up with the figure of 1.5 per cent. It is quite clear in the Budget that the Old Age Security benefits will not be automatically indexed quarterly, as they have been since 1972 or 1973, by whatever the increase in the cost of living has been in that quarter, but that in each year beginning January 1, 1986, there will be no indexation of the Old Age Security pensions for the first 3 per cent of the increase in the cost of living.
The increase in the cost of living is down right now. This year it is down dramatically from what it was a few years ago, but it is only down to 4 per cent. If it stays at 4 per cent next year, something which is doubtful, then people receiving Old Age Security benefits will have a reduction in their real purchasing power of 3 per cent. The Parliamentary Secretary tried to rationalize his position by saying that the reduction of 1.5 per cent would not be so serious because somehow senior citizens could purchase alternatives.
1 would like to bring to the attention of the Parliamentary Secretary an article which appeared in the Montreal Gazette, a newspaper which is neither radical nor revolutionary. This article appeared on May 24 of this year and the headline reads:
Budget hurts poor, consumer groups say.

Let me put on the record some of the things which Members of Parliament are hearing from senior citizens across the country. Let me begin with a communication which came from the New Brunswick Senior Citizens' Federation dated June 14, 1985, addressed to all Members of Parliament of Canada of all political Parties, all Members of the Senate of Canada, all provincial premiers and all senior citizens' associations across Canada. I am sure the Parliamentary Secretary knows that we terrible New Democrats do not have very much support in New Brunswick, so we cannot be accused of having fomented that. After all, the Conservatives won most of the seats in New Brunswick, so I do not know how the Liberals could have produced it. Someone must have done it. Maybe it was the senior citizens themselves. Despite the arguments of Conservative members, maybe the senior citizens of New Brunswick are not so stupid. Maybe they know what is happening.
I would like to read into the record what the senior citizens in New Brunswick wrote in a circular which was sent to all Members of Parliament. I presume the Parliamentary Secretary received a copy. The circular is from the New Brunswick Senior Citizens' Inc. It reads:
On June 5th, we held a media conference in Moncton to announce our plans to make everyone aware of the immorality and dishonesty of tampering with Canada's (already inadequate) pension system for the elderly.
We indicated that we would make waves from the Atlantic to the Pacific. This has indeed happened.
The circular continues:
New Brunswick senior citizens are a rare breed. There are 76,800 of them. Five hundred new retirees are added to statistics monthly.
Seventy-three per cent of them are below the poverty level (GIS). Tremendous numbers of these are single ladies and/or widows of lumbermen, fishermen or farmers.

I have a copy of a telegram which was sent to the Minister of National Health and Welfare and to the Minister of Finance a few days ago. The telegram was sent by the National Council of Jewish Women of Canada. That is a very hard-working group which has been in the forefront in urging improvements in the social security system of Canada for many years. The telegram reads:
National Council of Jewish Women of Canada representing 4,000 women presently meeting in Ottawa at its 23rd biennial convention urges the Government of Canada to continue the indexing of old age pensions. We oppose any measure which threatens the financial security of senior citizens in order to reduce the deficit.
We are beginning to hear from seniors. I received a telephone call in my office last week from the management of a large shopping mall in my constituency. They invited my assistant to go to the mall in order to obtain signatures for a petition which would oppose the deindexing of pensions. They told us that they would be quite happy to set up tables and chairs. They said that the only thing we could not do was put up a sign indicating that we were from the New Democratic Party.
I would like to read into the record the wording of the petition. 1 would like a Conservative Member of Parliament, who has been saying that we have been misrepresenting the facts to the seniors, to get up after I have finished and tell Members of the House how we are misrepresenting the facts and the situation as it will affect our senior citizens. The petition reads:
That in the opinion of your petitioners, the May 23 Budget imposes undue and unfair hardship on pensioners by deindexing the Old Age Security (OAS) program, and
That the annual cut to each and every OAS pensioner in Canada will be $100 in 1986, $205 in 1987, $315 in 1988, $431 in 1989, $553 in 1990 and $680 in 1991 and

That deindexing represents a massive withdrawal from our collective commitment to public pensions, indicating the Government favours shifting to a system of tax-subsidized private savings for retirement and That the losers will be the poor, the unemployed and women Wherefore, the undersigned your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon the House of Commons to reinstate full indexation of the Old Age Security program in Canada.
I would urge any Conservative Member of Parliament who believes that any statement of fact in that petition is not true to get up and tell the Members of the House why it is not true.
I was at the shopping mall with a few friends and workers last Friday afternoon from 4 p.m. to 8 p.m. We collected 1,500 signatures. The people not only signed their names, they also gave their addresses. Naturally, most of the people who signed the petition live in my constituency. However, people from the ridings of Winnipeg North Centre and Winnipeg-Birds Hill, which are represented by my colleagues, signed the petition.
As well, people from the riding of Winnipeg-Fort Garry, which is represented by a Liberal member, signed the petition. People from the ridings of Winnipeg-St. James, St. Boniface and Selkirk-lnterlake, which are Conservative ridings, signed the petition. 'Lo and behold, people from the riding of Provencher, which is represented by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, signed the petition.
Conservative members from Manitoba issued a press statement which said that they were not hearing from their constituents. Mr. Chairman, they are hearing from their constituents. They ought not to try to kid their constituents or anyone else that the senior citizens are not upset. 1 told the Hon. Member for Portage-Marquette, the Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board, that unless the Government changed its policy before Parliament recesses on June 28, that I would take a day or two in early July to visit some of the seniors in the towns of Portage la Prairie and Neepawa which are in his riding. I said that I would take the petition with me to see how many of those seniors would sign it. The Minister of State for the Canadian Wheat Board knows that many seniors will sign that petition. speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subtopic: PATENTS-REQUEST FOR DETAILS CONCERNING CLOSING OF PATENT OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on May 29, I addressed a question to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) on the dismantling of the Patent Office. It will be remembered that in the working paper tabled with the Budget and entitled 'New Management Initiatives', on page 21-this is the famous paper of the Hon. Deputy Minister of Canada (Mr. Nielsen), the following suggestion is made: The Government will suggest that the review of patents no longer be carried out by the federal administration and that the examination of patents originally filed in Canada should be contracted out to international research bodies.
Mr. Speaker, I was just paraphrasing an excerpt of that document, and I ask for your indulgence for reading through it a little hastily.
On May 29, I asked the Minister about the proposal made by the Nielsen Task Force. He told me at that time, and I quote:
-the Government is anxious to provide the best possible service at the lowest possible cost... and I can assure him that there are quite a few patent applications that must be examined before any employees can be laid off-

June 18, 1985
Adjournment Debate
In French he used the word "debauchage", but I assume this is correctly translated by "laid off'.
-and we must proceed with these applications before any final steps are taken.
Mr. Speaker, this answer suggests that he is in agreement with the recommendation made in that famous document issued by the Deputy Prime Minister of Canada (Mr. Nielsen). The question, then, is why is the Government seeking to dismantle the Canadian Patent Office and to have its work done by a foreign agency, which would do the research required to grant Canadian patents at the same time as research for other countries?
You will recall, Mr. Speaker, that in 1984-85, for example, 26,947 patent applications were received. More than 90 per cent of them were from abroad. How many people does the Patent Office employ? The jobs of 200 public servants are threatened by this measure. In 1983-84, revenues of the Patent Office amounted to $13,411,000, whereas expenses were only $9,266,000. So, profits for that year reached $4,145,000. These are public figures, Mr. Speaker, I did not make them up. They prove that it is a money making service, a profitable operation serving all Canadians.
The Patent Co-operation Treaty, which the Minister indicated would have to be signed following amendment in the House to the present legislation, was intended, in the words of the Minister, "to overcome the need for the examination of patents in those countries that adhered to the Treaty".
The signatories to the Treaty recognize that domestic laws vary from nation to nation and that each country must have ultimate control over its domestic patent laws and the patents granted thereunder.
The Patent Co-operation Treaty exists for the benefit of inventors who wish to file patent applications in a number of countries throughout the world. However, experience has shown that it is not economically viable for inventors to take advantage of the terms of the Treaty, unless protection is sought in more than five countries. In 1984, WIPO or the World Intellectual Property Organization office examined only 271 applications under the relevant section of the Treaty.
There would be consequences of the "Nielsen" recommendation concerning the abolishment or withdrawal of the service to Canadians. First, Canada would abdicate its sovereignty over its patent system and would become the only industrialized country in the world which grants patents without domestic examination. On the assumption that 25,000 persons per year still want patent protection in Canada, the staff of the Geneva-based organization will obviously have to be substantially increased, resulting in an export of jobs from Canada to Geneva, Switzerland. Trained professionals in Canada who are knowledgeable in patent law will disappear from the public sector and will substantially be reduced in number in the private sector. The quality and availability of advice to small
business will be substantially reduced. That would go against what I consider to be a promise of the Government to encourage small and medium-sized businesses.
What made this question very important was that the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Cote) said in a speech in Montreal that there was never any question of him abolishing this service. He said:
Let me state categorically that we have no intention whatsoever of closing the patent office. Nor have we the intention of letting go that substantial body of people whose technical and scientific expertise underpins one of the finest patent services in the world.
I say "hurrah" to the Minister. We have finally received an answer after several weeks of the Minister unknowingly leading people to think that he would close it down following the report entitled New Management Initiatives, by the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Defence (Mr. Nielsen).
What will the Minister do? Will he close it down or leave it open? Are we to take the Minister's word in Montreal, or are we to take the word of the Deputy Prime Minister?

speakeroldname: Mr. Bill Domm (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subtopic: PATENTS-REQUEST FOR DETAILS CONCERNING CLOSING OF PATENT OFFICE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I welcome the opportunity to deal with the matter of the Canadian Patent Office, because the Hon. Member who brought the subject forward discussed a possibility that was studied and a possibility indicated in a report. Again the Opposition is jumping to conclusions when it assumes, if someone studies something or takes something under consideration, that all things are final.
There has been a great deal of confusion about the future of the Canadian Patent Office in the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs since budget night. I want to clarify the situation. To begin with, let me make it perfectly clear that the Government has no intention of doing away with the patent office, nor does it have any intention of letting go, as has already been stated by the Hon. Member who is once again using the old policy of scare tactics, that substantial body of people.
This issue appears to have become magnified out of proportion. The Government intends to reduce our costs by accepting foreign examination results wherever possible. Indeed, this will, as indicated in the budget paper entitled New Management Initiatives, "terminate departmental examinations". However, this does not mean that it will close up the shop.
The confusion probably lies in the fact that the substantive patent examination process consists of three distinct phases, and the Hon. Member is referring to only one of them. One phase is the search, which is to identify earlier, similar inventions. The second stage is the preliminary examination, which is to decide if the invention merits a patent under Canadian law. It is steps one and two of this process which we intend to streamline, although a lot has been done in this regard in the last few years. By acceding to the Patent Co-operation Treaty the Government hopes to be even more efficient. Step three, on the other hand, is not something we can contract out to
June 18, 1985

foreigners and we have no intention of discontinuing that activity.
All of this means that the Patent Office will remain very much in business, doing those things that depend most on its Canadian scientific and technical expertise. There will certainly not be any wholesale dismissal of professional or support staff, nor will there be any reduction in the service offered to the business and scientific community. Indeed, as the Budget points out, we intend to improve our levels of service. Work has already started to find ways to best carry out another important announcement about patents made on budget night; the strengthening of the patent information dissemination through expanded use of the established network of the National Research Council's Canada Institute for Scientific and Technical Information.
We want to be certain that the Canadian patent system is as efficient and effective as possible in meeting our needs as a modern industrial nation. It must enhance transfer of technology between ourselves and the rest of the world, and it must continue to contribute to a strengthening of the climate for investment in Canada.

On two specific occasions the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) made two commitments. As a result of the Budget the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources has reneged on her commitment. It would not be appropriate for me to use the word used by some workers describing the Minister as a "liar". I would not use that word, Mr. Speaker, but that is what they call the Minister. There has been no consultation on the closure of those two heavy water plants, not withstanding the fact that the Minister promised the union responsible that there would be meaningful consultation. There has been no impact study of the effects that that will have in Glace Bay and Port Hawkesbury. I find it appalling that the Government of Canada would cut 700
Adjournment Debate
jobs, affecting approximately 300 people, without doing an impact study.
What has the Government done with regard to the closure of the two heavy water plants? The Hon. Member for Halifax West (Mr. Crosby) said that the closure of those plants would affect 3,000 jobs. The Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens) arrived in Cape Breton on his private jet. Before leaving Ottawa he said that thousands of new jobs will be created for the people who reside in eastern Nova Scotia. This jellyfish of a Minister said that the Government is going to upgrade a highway and build an industrial park in Antigon-ish. He said there would be a study with regard to Carbogel. He then went a little further in making another announcement that same day. He talked about having Magna International expand into Cape Breton. That will create another study, Mr. Speaker. I say shame on the Government, shame on the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, and shame on the jellyfish of a Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion. I say shame on the Prime Minister who has been referred to both by his own constituents and by workers in my riding as a liar. I say that this is hogwash. The Government ought to take specific action with moneys for Sydney Steel Corporation, the coal industry and a joint venture for the synfuels project. We do not need all government money but we need joint ventures.
The Government ought to conclude a federal-provincial subsidiary agreement on development in eastern Nova Scotia, to include research and development, tourism, fisheries, forestry, municipal infrastructures, small business entrepreneurs and training and education funds. That is what the Government ought to be doing rather than deceiving and, as the workers have said, lying to the people of Nova Scotia.

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: ENERGY-CLOSURE OF CAPE BRETON HEAVY WATER PLANTS- CREATION OF EMPLOYMENT. (B) REQUEST FOR GOVERNMENT ACTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Hon. Member is surely not a novice in politics. He has known for a long time about the crucial problems experienced by the heavy water plant of Atomic Energy of Canada in Cape Breton.

While federal Governments have been as supportive as possible to this industry which has historically been plagued with marketing problems linked to international conditions, the Government has taken decisive action in announcing the closure of these plants. The fact is that there exists a very

June 18, 1985
Adjournment Debate
major over-capacity in Canada's heavy water industry and no immediate solution to marketing difficulties is in view.
In these circumstances, the Government could no longer justify continuing operations at the plants. We found it unconscionable to maintain the status quo at a cost to taxpayers of $100 million per year. We believe that such action would not only have been unfair to the Canadian taxpayer but to heavy water plant workers. They knew that these closures were inevitable and that the indefinite perpetuation of operations would only delay the time when these plants could be replaced with viable long-term industrial activity in Cape Breton.
The Government decided to take the political risk and announce these closures in the May 1985 federal Budget. However, we have not abandoned the people of Cape Breton. As outlined in the Budget, workers will be provided with generous severance benefits, retraining and relocation assistance and financial and career counselling, together with measures designed to facilitate re-employment. In addition, the impact on the affected communities' property tax revenues will be offset for a specific period of time. Another Budget measure is the introduction of a special tax credit which will be instituted to enhance private-sector investment and productive employment in Cape Breton. This will result in no federal income tax being payable by investors for 10 to 15 years.
The unemployment triggered by the plant closures has been significantly offset by announcements made by the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion (Mr. Stevens). The Minister has announced that $1.5 million in federal funding has been designated to rebuild a burned out fish plant, $4.1 million has been committed for improvements to the Point Tupper pulp and paper mill, and $16 million has been earmarked for improved facilities in the coal mines. In addition, the Minister of Regional Industrial Expansion has appointed an advisory committee on economic development measures for Cape Breton Island, a committee which will start work immediately and submit its first report in September. The Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources (Miss Carney) has indicated that she is ready to assist in bringing economic renewal to Cape Breton through reliable, sound employment creation.
In conclusion, I would like to say that the Government does not enjoy playing the villain. However, when a very difficult problem exist we try to ameliorate it. Since 1982, AECL has been recommending the closure of the heavy water plants of Cape Breton. Since we came into power, we have studied the problem and the acceptable options considerably. We feel that we have made a responsible decision and put into place responsible measures which will put Cape Breton back on the road to economic renewal.

subtopic: FINANCE-INVESTMENT OF PENSION FUNDS-BUDGET PROPOSAL. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
FINANCE-INVESTMENT OF PENSION FUNDS-BUDGET PROPOSAL. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 5, I asked the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) two questions about the budget proposal which will allow Canadian pension funds to invest $3 abroad for every $1 invested in Canadian small business. I asked the Minister what consultation there had been with Canadians to establish that they were willing to have one-third of their retirement savings invested outside the Canadian economy. The only answer I received was that the people who administered the pension funds wanted this because it would enable them to earn a higher rate. That seemed like a strange answer.
My supplementary question concerned the possible impact, if the Government's three-to-one offer was taken up on a large scale, of an amount leaving Canada which could be as high as $28 billion.
Canadians have at least $90 billion in pension funds. The budget proposal would let pension funds invest up to 7 per cent of their assets in a new small business program, and three times as much, or 21 per cent, in foreign investments. Prior to this, pension funds could invest a maximum of 10 per cent of their assets in foreign investments. With the addition of 21 per cent, there is now a maximum of 31 per cent. The House has just passed the Government's Investment Canada Bill, which throws the country wide open to unfettered foreign ownership, allegedly to create jobs. Nevertheless, apparently the Government is prepared to accept, with equanimity, a flow of capital out of Canada to create jobs elsewhere.
The Minister of State for Finance answered my question about the impact on the Canadian economy of a massive capital outflow, if the program was taken up. She said:
Mr. Speaker, I assume that the Hon. Member is suggesting that $10 billion invested in Canadian small business is a bad thing.
It is getting increasingly hard to take this Government's dismissive attitude toward serious questions which are asked by the Official Opposition. This is a serious matter and it should be dealt with seriously.
Companies are now being set up. It is happening. Pension funds have generally invested in very traditional kinds of investments. The new companies, which will act as a channel for investment in Canadian small business, will, we trust, bring expertise to entrepreneurial and higher risk investments. We have no guarantee that there will be any limits, other than the percentages which I previously quoted.
I do not understand the Minister's answer that pension funds want this because they can get a higher rate of interest outside Canada. That is a terrible admission of failure. If the Minister is saying that pension funds do not believe they can get a satisfactory rate within Canada, are we to understand that the Government is completely abdicating any improvement in the Canadian economy?
The other point to which I believe we are entitled to an answer is, will the Government be doing any monitoring? Will there be any kind of sensible limits placed on the program? Are we to assume that we again have the kind of open-ended measure which will be demand-driven, which will take on an impetus of its own, and which will leave us possibly facing undesirable consequences down the road?
June 18, 1985

speakeroldname: Mr. Claude Lanthier (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: FINANCE-INVESTMENT OF PENSION FUNDS-BUDGET PROPOSAL. (B) MINISTER'S POSITION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the government is worried because pension funds have been slow to invest in Canadian small businesses. However, pension fund assets in Canada now total about $100 billion. Acording to some estimates, only $200 to $300 million, that is one quarter of one per cent, have been invested in limited partnerships. The government has therefore committeed itself to guarantee that a larger part of those funds will be made available to small businesses.
The Budget tries to overcome the lack of interest shown by pension funds by proposing three measures. The first two involve the creation of new institutions, small business investment corporations and small business investment limited partnerships, to facilitate investments. Pension funds will then be allowed to use those vehicles to co-ordinate the research and administration of their investments in small business and thus provide them with limited responsibility.
The third measure would encourage pension funds to make good investments in the small business sector. For each dollar invested in a Canadian small business, these funds will be allowed to invest $3 abroad.
Adjournment Debate
It is true pension funds can invest 7 per cent of their assets in so-called basket investments which, of course, can include investments in small businesses. It is also true that in so doing, another 21 per cent of the assets of these funds could theoretically go to foreign investments.
It is not presently possible to determine how much of this theoretical limit will in fact be used if all basket-type funds are invested in small businesses. However, if pension funds take full advantage of this opportunity, if they invest up to the theoretical limit, they would provide a tremendous economic stimulus to Canadian small business.
The Government will closely monitor the impact of foreign investments by pension funds as well as their direct effects on the economy. If any problems arise, corrective measures will be taken immediately.
Because these measures will encourage investment in the more productive businesses and in high growth firms, we are confident they will contribute to increase productivity and create more jobs for Canadians.
